Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct the attention of the government to an article that appears in last Saturday's Montreal Herald, written by Mr. Devlin, and dated from the Canadian Government Office in the city of Dublin. That article contains a very strong criticism on certain members of this House. As a rule, I do not pay any attention to what is said about me in the newspapers, but having been criticised by the same gentleman on the 11th of May, in United Canada, I wish to say that if Mr. Devlin has tbe right to criticise Members of this parliament. I presume every official in the civil service has the same right. If one official has that right, then all should have it, and every civil servant should be entitled to criticise any member of this House.
Did he tell the truth ?

No, he did not. It is not worth while to enter into the details at this late period of the session, of Mr. Devlin's statements, but if I am spared, I expect to be able to show at some future time, that either Mr. Devlin or the reports of the Department of the Interior are entirely wrong. I simply want to call the attention of the government to the fact that Mr. Devlin, a public servant, is criticising certain members of this House, that he has done so unfairly, and that in fact he has made untruthful statements. As it is so near the end of the session, I do not wish to take up any more of the time of the House.

I expressed my opinion on this subject the other day in Committee of Supply, and I have nothing to say in justification of the course adopted by the gentleman referred to. I will endeavour to see that no official in my department offends in that direction again.

I have asked by notice of motion for certain papers and correspondence between the government of Canada and the people of the county of Pontiac, in regard to the railway indebtedness of that county. Many lion, gentlemen will remember that in 1891 I was elected for the county I have now the honour to represent. This question of the railway indebtedness of the county has been before the people for many years. The people of Pontiac unfortunately voted a large bonus in 1881, to the Pontiac Pacific Junction Railway. to be paid under certain conditions which were not fulfilled by the company.

The county resisted payment, and the result was that they got involved in a much larger debt, the amount with interest being in all about $200,000. The question came before the people at various elections, and the government candidate as a rule said : ' Vote for the government candidate and get relieved from the bonus.' In that way the county was carried for the late Conservative government for many years. In 1S91 there were three candidates in the field, namely, the late Mr. John Bryson, the Conservative candidate. Mr. Maclean, Independent candidate, and myself, the Liberal candidate. Both my opponents had certain advantages over me, as they said they had the ear of the government if they should be returned to power. I stated to the electors that so far as I could I would do all that was possible for the public in regard to that question, and in regard to every other question affecting their welfare. At all events, I was elected, but I was unseated in the courts, and the late Mr. John Bryson was a candidate against me in the by-election. He would not accept the nomination of his friends until he interviewed the government of the day to know what they would likely do in regard to this question.

I rise to a point of order. I do not think that the time of the House should be wasted at this late stage of the session. The hon. gentleman is discussing a question, a motion with respect to which is on the Order paper.

I was going on to say that the late Mr. John Bryson stated at the by-election, that he had interviewed the government and that he had a promise from the government that they would relieve the county from this railway debt. Hence it is that I moved for this information. Pontiac is a large county, requiring development und colonization, and this debt, which is a heavy burden on the people, is calculated to retard our progress. The county council has sent a memorial to the government, asking for the desired relief. I think the exMinister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Haggart) will remember that this question was brought before the attention of the Conservative government, and he will know whether any promise or intimation was given which would warrant the people in expecting that they would get this relief. When I was a member of this House before, although I was in opposition to the then government, I interviewed Sir John Thompson in his own office, and I frankly state that the late Sir John Thompson was personally disposed to do something to relieve the county of Pontiac in this matter. I am now endeavouring to discharge my duty to my constituents in bringing this question to the attention of parliament. I say that it is but an act of justice for this administration, or any administration, to come to the rescue of the people of Pontiac, who are so handicapped by this very heavy financial burden. This debt has the effect of not only preventing new colonists coming into the county, but it tends to drive our people who are already there out of the county. 1 do not wish to take up any more time at this late period of the session, but I would mention that the hon. member for Guysborougli (Mr. Eraser) was at the nomination in Pontiac, and I think he will remember well that the late John Bryson stated there, openly and above board, ' Vote for me, and I will get you relief from the debt, and if I do not do that within a year, I will hand back your mandate.' It is no wonder that I was handicapped and defeated by a pretty large majority in the last by-election. I do not want to say any more on this subject. The members of the county council have memorialized the present administration, and I hope that they will give the matter the consideration it deserves, and that next session they will decide to relieve the county of its present burden of railway indebtedness.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I wish to put a question to the government in connection with a petition
which asks for the disallowance of an Act passed at the last session of the legislature of Quebec. I have brought to the notice of the right hon. gentleman the facts relating to the position taken by the petitioners in the matter, and I have also communicated to him for his own information, and for the information of the Department of Justice, a memorial which was prepared in support of that petition.
I do not intend to take up the time of the House in discussing the matter, as there remains a great deal of business to be gone through with before prorogation day. The facts of the case are quite familiar to all those who have watched the provincial legislation. We all know that law of exception which debars petitioners, in many cases, from the right of proceeding with the trial of the election petitions which they have commenced, and which also forbids entering an action before a court of criminal jurisdiction. In their petition, the petitioners deliver all particulars and give all the necessary explanations as to the facts of the case. If I refer to this matter I do so at the request of the interested parties, in order to call the attention of the government to that petition and to ask the right hon, prime minister to see to it that this petition be given due consideration, should it be referred to tile Department of Justice.
Feople are apt to think that the power of disallowance applies only to laws which are ultra vires of the province ; but those who are familiar with the matter know very well that such is not the case. As a matter of fact, we find sufficient protection in the courts from laws which are ultra vires of the province. The power of disallowance applies still more forcibly to laws which encroach upon vested rights, and which interfere with public policy of the country, although such laws are intra vires of the province.
As set forth in the petition in question, the legislation referred to interferes with the two principles I have just alluded to. In the first place, that law prevents the courts from taking cognizance of six and, I believe even seven, election petitions entered in due time, but which were stayed during the session of the provincial legislature. Were the legislation to which I call the attention of the government to be maintained, the result would be that the petitioners would be deprived of the right of proceeding with their cases, and they would incur heavy legal costs. Moreover, in each of these cases, it is set forth that corrupt practices have prevailed ; and that those elections were not conducted in a proper and regular way, and that the candidate returned was not the free choice of the electorate.
It seems to me, Sir. that by thus staying the trial of those election petitions and by depriving the petitioners of the privilege of enforcing their rights, you strike a blow at public morality under such circumstances.

I hope that the petition in question will receive due consideration at the hands ol' the executive. The right lion. Prime Minister has no doubt remarked that in the concluding portion of the memorial which I placed in his hands many authorities are quoted which have a direct bearing upon the case which is now referred to the executive for consideration. Those authorities are taken from Hodgins ' Dominion and Provincial Legislation, 1867-95.'
I shall not take up the time of the House quoting those authorities. Let it suffice to say that those authorities show beyond the shadow of a doubt that the power of disallowance has often been exercised by the Governer General in Council. And surely, If the power of disallowance can be resorted to when vested rights are encroached upon, and when attempts are made to prevent the courts from taking cognizance of questions which are still sub juiUce, it is under such circumstances as those referred to.
I may call the attention of the House to the fact that the Attorney General of the province of Quebec, so far as my information goes, voted against that law. That goes to show that the Attorney General shared in the opinion given expression to in the petition asking for the disallowance of the Act referred to.
I hope that this petition will receive due consideration at the hands of the government.

It is not within my knowledge that any such petition has been received by the Governor General. If it has been presented, it must have been within the last few days, as I am sure it has not yet been referred to the Privy Council.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: I may state that I handed the petition to the Secretary of State myself, and he gave me a written acknowledgment, which I sent to the petitioner, and in which I think he stated that it was about to be put into the hands of the government.

That must have been within a very few days, for I am sure it has not yet been submitted to the Privy Council. Perhaps it has been referred to the Minister of Justice, and the Minister of Justice has not yet made his report upon it. However, my hon. friend has been kind enough to give me communication of the petition, which asks for the disallowance of the Act to which he has referred. In the memorial which has been placed in my hands, coming, not from several petitioners, but from Mr. Nantel himself, he states that he was a candidate in the election which took place on the 7th of December last in the county of Terrebonne, and was declared not elected, and that he entered a petition under the Controverted Elections Act against the return of liis opponent. His Interest, therefore, is to have the law set aside, so that the petition which he has Mr. MONK.
placed in the hands of the court may be proceeded with. Without going into the merits of the case, perhaps my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has noticed already that even if the Act were to be disallowed, Mr. Nantel could derive no benefit from that disallowance, because, according to the memorial which has been placed in my hands, a judgment of the court, pronounced by Mr. Justice Taschereau, has been rendered between the parties, sitting aside all the proceedings, and declaring the petition to be null and void. Under such circumstances, even if the Act were disallowed, I do not believe Mr. Nantel could revive that petition, which is res judicata between the parties. My hon. friend is right in saying that the power of disallowance applies not only to laws which are ultra vires of the province, but more forcibly still to laws which are intra vires of the province ; because, as he suggests, laws which are ultra vires of the province do not require to be disallowed, because the courts will set them aside when their attention is called to them. This law was certainly within the powers of the legislature of Quebec. Whether the legislature acted wisely or unwisely, I am not prepared at this moment to say ; but if I were to express an opinion, I would say that if I had been in the legislature, I would have voted with the Attorney General of the province against the law. But that law lifts no effect, so far as the election in the county of Terrebonne is concerned, the judge having set aside the petition and all the "proceedings ; and if we were to disallow the Act, the disallowance would only apply to other sections of the community where elections are pending ; but we have received ino petition from anybody that I know of except Mr. Nantel, and I submit, with all due deference, that he has no more interest in the matter.
With regard to the representations made by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Murray), I have only to say that so far as my information goes, after searches made in the department, we find nothing to warrant the statement made in the election in the county of Pontiac, that the government of ' the day were to come to the rescue of the people of Pontiac. If such a promise was made by the late government or by any government of Canada, of course we shall be happy next session to bring down the papers.

Rut we are advised that the lowering to this extent will amply sufllce to give us the due supply of water. We are dropping the mitre sill one foot lower than at present.
Galops Canal-Enlargement, $90,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We have in the main estimates for the current year a vote of $330,000, so, that this will make a total of $420,000 for this purpose.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

Lachine Canal-Towards building new lock, $500,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What does this mean ?

I presume that the hon. gentleman does not remember the explanation that I gave when the vote was given last session, so I will restate it. There are two locks at this point, at the mouth of the Lachine canal, which are in a very dilapidated condition. One is so much disabled that it would be a waste of money to attempt to repair it, and it must be rebuilt if the locks there are to be continued. We have invited tenders for a contract for a lock 600 feet in length. Wc thought it well to adopt the plan of substituting a long and large lock, knowing what might possibly occur in the way of desiring to have large steamers go through our canals. At all events, in this particular instance we ask for tenders upon that basis. The lock will be 600 feet long, 50 feet wide, and with 20 feet of water on the mitre sill. We have not awarded the contracts yet. Some question has arisen,

since we invited tenders, as to whether it would be possible to make arrangements with the Harbour Board of Montreal for the utilization of their guard pier at Windmill Point, which would inclose a magnificent basin. We would like to utilize that, and have a lock at the end of it. That subject is under consideration now, but, owing to press of business towards the close of the session, we have not yet been able to consult with the harbour authorities on the subject, but we hope to very soon. We desire to satisfy ourselves whether or not it would be possible to carry on our work in that direction.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I entirely approve of making this lock, because it increases the harbour accommodation of the city of Montreal. especially for vessels bringing coal up to the city. The depth should be at least 20 feet on the mitre sill, I think we ought to make it 20 feet and 6 inches. X do not know whether a breadth of 50 feet would be sufficient. But, I would like him to make the breadth of the locks correspond with the locks on the proposed Georgian Bay canal, in case we ever have there a new inland system of canals. I think 20 feet of depth is hardly sufficient, because the water varies so much in the St. Lawrence below. I think all the new locks on the Lachine canal were built of that size. I presume the depth above the locks for a certain distance will be 22 feet.
Building slope walls, dredging pontoon gate, power-house enlargement, $86,000.
The slope walls are on the enlarged and deepened portion of the canal ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

$2.50. We estimate .$10,000 for the slope walls, $20,000 for dredging.
Trent Canal, $141,500.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

I gave some figures on that subject when we were discussing the main estimates. I could get them again for the hon. gentleman, but he will find them in the 1 Hansard.'
Lachine Canal-To pay a proportion of the cost of paving Mill street, $20,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why is this ?

This is all on our own ground. We have been repairing it from time to time, and have taken periodical votes for that purpose. But, it is in very bad condition,
and we think it will be more economical to pave it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is not land along the basin, it is a public street of the city of Montreal.

No, they will not take it, they do not recognize it. If the hon. gentleman can suggest some method by which we can give up the control of a highway that we have been maintaining for years, and which has not been taken over by the municipality, so that we may avoid responsibility for it,
I would be very glad indeed. It is between the canal and the river, some distance away, with a number of buildings alongside of it, and these people must have access to it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Could the hon. gentleman say whether our canal extends the whole way alongside of it ?
Yes, certainly, right along. Do you know where the Pillow-Hersey Company is located ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Yes. That is on a portion of the street across the Wellington street bridge.
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. No, it is not there at all.

This is a street that runs up alongside of the canal.
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. It is on the side of the canal between the river and the canal.

Would the hon. gentleman explain what the total cost of the paving is and who is paying the balance ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	ANDCANALS. I believe	the cost of	paving is estimated to be in the neighbourhood of $50,000.

Yes, but it says :
To pay a proportion of the cost of paving Mill street.
What is the proportion ?

The decision of counsel is to say to the municipality that we will be prepared to contribute this amount towards paving the whole of the street if they will take it over and assume the balance and we will be done with it. We have been discussing this matter for a very long time and we thought this would be the most satisfactory mode of bringing the question to an end.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Then, the municipality is to take the street over ?
noTvnvroNS
Yes, and assume the responsibility for it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Responsibility for keeping it in repair in future V
For maintenance in future. That is our proposal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The proposal of the government is that this shall be the last contribution ?

That is the proposal that we are proposing to make. We have not made it yet but council has decided upon asking parliament to make this appropriation upon the understanding that anything oyer this amount shall be met by the municipality. We have not decided, nor is it our present purpose, to spend any portion of the money unless and until the municipality agrees to accept the offer and to take the road off our hands on these terms.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think this is a most exceptional thing to do and that it is an odd situation that we find ourselves in. We have government property, the municipality 'requires it, and we have no further need of it, the municipality is using it. and we propose to give it over to the municipality but we do not propose to give it over until we have spent $20,000 on it. We are not only making a gift but we are proposing to add to the gift by spending public money. It seems to me that it would be a proper thing to give the roadway over to the municipality and let the municipality keep it up. What right has the country to keep it up. What right have we to add to the gift by spending $20,000 as an inducement for the municipality to take it over ?

You have to look at things pretty much as they are. You cannot entirely obliterate what has occurred before. We have been recognized as being answerable, whether rightly or wrongly, for the condition of this highway. We have been spending $2,000 a year in keeping it in repair. We have our own workshops on it and the public must have access to these shops, while other people have established businesses there and they also have to have access to the property occupied by them. At the outset, I suppose, we required that this highway should be opened for our own convenience and later it was found also to be necessary for the convenience of the public, and recognizing this, we have been paying from year to year for keeping it up. It looks to me a somewhat serious matter that we should be burdened with the responsibility. year after year, of spending $2,000, or $3,000, upon it and it occurred to us that if we could make an arrangement with the municipality whereby it would
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: take this road over and assume the entire responsibility of maintaining it, it would be a very excellent business arrangement to do that.

If I remember rightly, I was down there one time and I saw men excavating rock from the canal, and drawing the rock and placing it upon this particular portion of the street. I was wondering what business we had to be macadamizing it at all and I stopped them. I believe the municipal authorities took the stone that was delivered on the road and did the work themselves. I never could understand what business we had to do any thing at all upon the street.
If this roadway is for general use what reason have we to spend money upon it at all ?
We may require it for our own purposes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If it is necessary to have this thoroughfare as a means of access 1o to our own shops there might be some reason for it, but if it is for the public convenience I do not see what justification there is for it.

We have leased a good deal of our land along the highway at fairly remunerative rentals to people who have taken this land, have put up buildings and have established themselves there, and they must have access to these buildings.
Macadamizing road from Cote St. Paul, $2,500. Hon. Mr. IIAGGART. Is that for the approaches to the bridge ? Surely this part is part of the city's work.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We have made appropriations, just how much I cannot say, at this moment-perhaps the deputy minister will know-In connection with this work. It is claimed when this canal was built that we should have macadamized this road which was established in connection with the canal. We either diverted or interfered with some other highway and we provided this highway in place of it and it is contended that we should make the highway serviceable. That claim has been recognized and we voted money for macadamizing the road in previous years. There is another portion that we propose to macadamize out of this vote.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
All I have to say is that the municipality of the city of Montreal ought to do this. When we went to the expense of building bridges the municipality ought to pay for the expense of macadamizing the road, instead of having to keep the road up in perpetuity.
To repair tug Frank Perew, $2,500.
What tug is that V

Yes, this tug came to us in connection with the property we took over from Mr. Stewart and it requires some repairs.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

My deputy says that they handed the tug back in the same condition they received it.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

The timber is rotten and the walls will be restored to their original height.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

Not a great deal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The total cost must be enormous. Who is the contractor ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. Martin Hogan Sons, and Le-moine.

Was there a tender for this canal ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. Yes.
Trent Canal-Towards rebuilding bridge over Chemong lake, $10,000.

Is this work under contract now ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. The bridge is pretty nearly completed. We are contributing towards the cost.
Is it the policy of the government to build all the bridges over the canals ?
No, Sir.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then why are you doing it in this case ?

I have endeavoured to avoid responsibility for any bridges that we are not directly charged with. When the government raised the dam here the water was raised so as to render the old bridge of no use. The municipality has to construct a new and a higher bridge, and we thought that in justice we should pay a part of the cost.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In the absence of the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Kendry). who is very familiar with this, I. may lie permitted to say a word. What the minister says is correct. Chemong lake is between Peterborough and Victoria counties, and before the water was raised for canal purposes the people from the western side of the lake had free access over the old bridge. This bridge has been rendered absolutely useless by the raising of the water, and I believe the government would be in a court of justice liable for the whole cost of this new bridge. They are perfectly right in asking for this vote.

I pointed out to the municipality that they would be getting a new bridge instead of the old one, and I thought that 25 per cent of the estimated cost would be a fair proportion for us to contribute.
Welland Canal-To rebuild dam and bridge at Iiunnville, $43,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This dam is in a very dilapidated condition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What use is a dam or bridge to you there ?

You cannot hold the water there and furnish a proper supply under the leases that we have granted, unless you repair that dam. The lessees have expressed much dissatisfaction. Some of them have not paid any rents for water for three years, and if I can carry out my intention, I propose to have all these rentals adjusted as a condition precedent to our assuming liability in connection with these dams.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why don't you have your rents readjusted before going on with the expenditure ? If we have several thousand dollars uncollected, and if we add to that by spending several thousand more it makes it worse.

I hope to have the whole thing established on a satisfactory business basis. There will be new leases and the quantity of water adjusted. Some claim that under their leases they can use more than they are entitled to, and all complain that the condition of the dam is such that the water runs away and that they cannot get the quantity they contracted for. Consequently they insist that they ought not to be asked for rent.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What was the amount you expended on it last year ?
We did not expend very much last year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You had a large gang at work during the elections, fixing up the dam.
You can put a large gang on for a day or two without spending a great *deal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: All I have to say is that this is an enormous amount of money to spend on a dam that is perfectly useless. It was formerly used for the purpose of supplying water from the Grand river to the feeder of the Welland canal but that feeder has been done away with, and the supply of water is now being taken from Lake Erie. It is true, there are a couple of little mills there, one owned by a former member for Haldimand, a supporter of the government ; but I venture to say that the amount these mill-owners have agreed to pay for the water power is not a tithe of the interest on the cost of the improvements which you propose to make this year. I do not think you will get $1,000 a year from them, or anything like it. An expenditure of $43,000 is an enormous expenditure on a work which is of a purely municipal cliarac-Iter. It is not of the slightest benefit to the government. It is wholly in the interest of a couple of Individuals, and I think is entirely unjustifiable.

What obligation rests on us to build a bridge at all ?
The' MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. The main cost will be the reconstruction of the dam. To make a bridge with a highway over it will not substantially increase the cost.
What is the necessity of building the dam at all ?

My hon. friend knows that after any public work has been in operation for a long time, and industries have grown up in the locality as a consequence, it is not possible, without raising a rebellion, to stop the maintenance of the work, even if you could Mr. SPROULE.
make a fine technical argument to prove that there was no absolute public need of it. Moreover, these people have taken leases from us, and have established their mills.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You say they are not paying their rent.

They have not been, because the water has been running away, and they have not been getting the supply which they had reason to expect we would furnish them. Year by year this dam has been getting into a worse state of repair, and water has been diminishing, and year by year these industries have been becoming injured ; and it has come to be a question whether or not we shall maintain this dam as originally [DOT]contemplated, or let it all go. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman, if he were in my position, would like to take the responsibility of saying that it should not be maintained, but should be allowed to fall into decay, and that these people, who are our lessees, and who put up these mills, should be left to shift for themselves. I, at any rate, do not feel like taking that responsibility, and it seems to me that the amount of expenditure necessarily involved in this work would not be sufficient reason to justify us in taking any such course as my hon. friend suggests.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If it were necessary for the purpose of keeping the water in the canal, this darn should be maintained ; but, as the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals says, that reason does not exist to-day, but that the dam is only for the purpose of making a water power for the benefit of the locality, it seems to me that it would be better for the government to sell it out by tender to some individual or private company, and let them maintain the power themselves.

Do I understand my hon. friends opposite strenuously to oppose this vote as one that cannot be justified ? If they say so, we will consider the proposition. My hon. friends know the situation. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways, has probably heard the hon. member who last represented Haldimand in this House most pressingly urge on the government that we should build this work as a necessary and important work, the failure to maintain which would lead to disaster to the community and to the industries established there. If my hon. friends opposite say that they are strenuously opposed to this vote, I will allow it to stand, and consider the matter.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister says that I heard my late colleague from Haldimand urge the rebuilding of this work. I do not remember anything of the kind.
I do.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not think ' Hansard ' will bear out the hon. gentleman's statement. I know the place as well as I do the bridge down here. The work is of no use at all except in the interest of a couple of mills, and I protest against the expenditure of the enormous sum of $43,000 upon it. If you feel yourselves morally bound, on account of these two particular mills, to keep the work in repair, let there be an arrangement with the mill-owners by which they will do the work themselves. The only liability you have to the municipality is this : by building a dam across there, you entail an increased expenditure on the municipality for the building of the road, and to that the government ought to contribute ; but if you take away the dam and leave the place as it was before in the course of nature, you have no right to contribute anything. The only question with the minister is whether he is morally bound to keep up the dam for the sake of these two establishments.
I think there are more than two.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There are two flour mills and an electric apparatus which provides electricity for the town.
The hon. gentleman made that lease himself.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I made it conditional on the surplus water not being required. If the hon. gentleman thinks that the government is morally bound, on account of the leases, to keep up this dam, he will find it a very expensive work. All I "can say that it is of no further use as a feeder of the canal, and its only use is for the purpose of supplying powers to these industries.
This dam was built by the late government as a public work. Do I understand my hon. friend to say that the late government committed an error ?
No, but the principle of supplying water from the Grand river a canal is abandoned, and there is no further use for this dam as a feeder of the canal.
This dam was built as a public work, and a condition of things has arisen under which it benefits the whole community. We are asked to let the work go out of repair altogether.
I do not go that far.

I am not proposing to spend anything more than is necessary to put this
dam into proper shape. We cannot expect the lessee to do this, but once it is in proper repair I am led to believe, by conversation with them, that they would willingly agree to keep it in repair. No reasonable person however would assume the burden of repairing it in its present condition. It has been allowed to fall into such decay that a large sum will be required to put it into proper shape.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister is then willing to spend $43,000 in repairing a dam which is of no benefit to the public at large but simply to accommodate two or three mills. The owners of these mills have been the lessees of the government and have not been paying any rent, and we are now told that it would be too onerous an imposition on them to ask them to keep that dam in repair, which furnishes them with their water power. When the hon. minister tells us that the late representative (Mr. Montague) urged the government last session the advisability of improving that work, he resorted to a very flimsy argument. I do not think he is so sensible to importunities on this side as he has shown himself to be to the appeal of the late hon. member for Haildimand. I think that there is a nigger on the fence and that the money is spent for another object than the benefit of the Canadian public.

The hon. minister has asked if we will take the responsibility of letting that dam go to the dogs. I frankly confess that I would. If it is no longer needed to supplement the water in the Welland canal, there is no reason why we should be saddled with the expense of keeping it up. The proper thing will be to sell out that power.
What rental do you get now ?	.

It is about $300 a year for the whole thing.

CANALS. We get something from the electric people.

Do they pay it ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. No.

Have they ever paid ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. I do not think so.
What portion of the $43,000 to be spent on the dam and what on the bridge ?
$25,000 for the dam, the bridge $8,000, and the temporary structure $7,000.

According to the engineers, you must have a temporary structure before you can reconstruct the present dam.

speechtext: Before the general discussion on this item takes place, I would like to draw the attention of the minister to a matter with respect to which I have had some correspondence. In 1896, one John B. McLellan, of Kingsville, Cape Breton, owned about 6,000 railway ties at West Bay road, River Dennis, and intermediate stations on the Cape Breton Railway. During the summer of 1896, the employees of the government on that railway came and loaded these ties on cars and carried them away to some place unknown to the owner. The owner alleged that he never parted with the title of these ties, or authorized any person to take possession of them. He is led to believe that some other person has been paid for them. He has had some correspondence with respect to the matter, but he is unable to get any satisfaction. If that is the case. T think the matter deserves immediate investigation on the part of the department. Of course. Mr. McLellan is entitled to be paid for his ties, the government has taken possession of them, and if the price has been paid to some one else, evidently an injustice has been done.
When did this occur ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Apparently in the summer of 1896, after the election. The number of ties, as stated to me by a reliable person, is 8,000. The facts, of which of course I have no personal knowledge, have been detailed to me by a solicitor in whose hands Mr. McLellan has placed the matter for the purpose of endeavouring to obtain some redress. Of course, yon may say that he might file a petition of right. But if the circumstances are as I have mentioned, I think it is a matter the government should immediately investigate, and endeavour to do justice to this man whose property appears to have been taken, either through mistake or otherwise, and paid for by the government to some other person. I have no doubt the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. McLennan) knows something of the matter, and I would be glad if he would make a fuller statement.
I have not heard an explanation from the minister about the Bob-caygeon dam.
I will endeavour to get a statement of the facts concerning these ties from my deputy minister. The matter has not been brought to my notice.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I did not expect the hon. gentleman would be able to give much information about it without notice. But I would be glad if he will take the matter into consideration and do what seems to be right.
I will.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Borden) has asked me what I know of this matter. The gentleman in question did apply to me to see what could be done re this matter, and I wrote to the department in his behalf. This gentleman sold these ties to the Boston and Nova Scotia Company, who in turn sold them to the Department of Railways. In answer to my letter the department replied that they had bought a certain number of ties from the Boston and Nova Scotia Company, at West Bay Road station, on the Intercolonial Railway, but the department could not say who originally owned the ties. Mr. McLellan sold these ties to the Boston and Nova Scotia Company, who forgot to pay him for them. When Mr. McLellan applied to me, I remember distinctly that I wrote to him advising him to forbid the government employees at West Bay station taking away the ties. He did so. He tells me he went to the station and forbade the government employees taking the ties away, warning them that he was going to apply to the Department of Railways for payment for these ties, having not been paid for them. The trackmen took the ties away, declaring that they knew nothing about the transaction between him and the Boston and Nova Scotia Company. From what I can gather from the department, the department certainly paid the Boston and Nova Scotia Company for the ties, but the company never paid Mr. McLellan for them. McLellan now. appeals through his solicitor to the department for redress. I must say that while the Department of Railways and Canals is innocent in the matter, it is a very hard case for Mr. McLellan, who honestly paid for the ties to the people who furnished them. There is an item, I believe, that the money was paid to Messrs. Fraser & Ross of the Boston and Nova Scotia Company.

Would the minister answer the hon. member for South Victoria, Ontario (Mr. Vrooman) with regard to the Bobcaygeon dam ?
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND
CANALS. It is pretty well understood that



the responsibility of maintaining the Bob-caygeon dam devolves upon the Department of Public Works or upon this department, it would probably be my department, so far as the dredging is concerned. I think it might be done without an express appropriation for the purpose. If the expenditure was not a very heavy one, and if the department decided that something should be done in the way of restoring that dam, it could be done without asking for an appropriation.

The dam belongs to the Department of Railways and Canals, there is no doubt about that. But the custom Is, as the minister says, to maintain it, not by a special vote, but from the general vote for the Trent canal.

We are asking for this vote in order to avail ourselves of the services of a. competent person to secure information of the way railways are operated in the different parts of Canada, and also, perhaps, to get similar information from the United States, so that when we come to frame a law for the establishment of a Railway Commission we may be equipped with full information for that purpose. It will be necessary, I think, to employ some gentleman of special competency and legal experience to prepare the Bill.
Cornwall Canal-In full settlement of Gilbert Dredging Company's claim (revote, $10,500), $16,480.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The committee will be glad to have some explanation from the hon. gentleman as to this $10,480, which it is proposed to pay as a settlement of the Gilbert Dredging Company's claim.

I may explain to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) that this is a revote. It will be found in the appropriations that we voted last year, but, notwithstanding the very full discussion which took place when this matter was under consideration, and in which all the various items constituting the total sum were fully explained, the Auditor General has, in the interim, since the vote was passed by parliament, hesitated, and not only hesitated, but refused, to make this payment. The vote has lapsed, and we are obliged now to obtain a revote in order that the claim may be paid. I need not go into the technical details, or make a new statement of the question which was the subject of controversy. We had it, I think, pretty well threshed out a year ago, and we have had more or less information, argument and correspondence directed to the subject by the Auditor General. The result has been that the Auditor General, who appears to me to imagine that he ought to know a great deal better than parliament as to whether this sum is a proper sum to be voted or not, has refused to make the payment. We have asked parliament to
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: revote the sum. We have carefully and fully considered the whole question, and we have had the opinion of the Department of Justice upon it. We have considered all the arguments which have been urged why it should not be paid, and we have gone into the whole question just as fully as if parliament had not voted the amount last year and as if it were a new question, and the result is that we have concluded that we are justified in asking for this sum to be revoted.

I suppose, Mr. Chairman, after the very full discussion of. last year and after it being shown beyond all doubt that there was no justification for the course the hon. gentleman took, to have called it a job, would have been to have paid it a compliment. I suppose it would now be unprofitable to renew the discussion upon the whole thing, but it is not without profit to consider whether the hon. gentleman is going to utterly disregard an officer of parliament, fortunately not under the control of the hon. gentleman, but whom he overrules time and again, and when he cannot overrule him by any decent mode of procedure he comes to parliament and asks for a justification on a ground of that kind. It it hardly worth discussing for a moment the importance of sustaining the financial officer of this parliament. If the government are going to overrule this officer on every conceivable ground, we may just as well dispense with the Auditor General altogether. So far as it weakens his influence for the useful purpose that he was intended to serve at the outset when parliament gave him great scope, it is a most serious thing for the hon. gentleman to make the proposal that he now makes. The Auditor General does not stand alone in this contention. He took very proper ground. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman now that he is proposing to force this vote through parliament-if he thinks it a proper thing to do, and X hope he will not go so far as to force it through when the Auditor General has behind him the opinion of Mr. Lash. The Auditor General has sought legal advice to fortify him in addition to his own long experience, and he is sustained in the position he takes. I would ask the hon. gentleman if he is going to permit such an outrage as to propose now to ask parliament to revote this sum to be paid to the Gilbert Dredging Company ? We cannot have a more serious question really than the payment of this sum of money standing alone. We have come to the point when a minister, rightly or wrongly, undertakes to force his own will against that of the Auditor General. I am not going to lay down the general principle that the Auditor General is always right, but the Auditor General has taken every means to set himself right so far as obtaining legal advice upon the question is concerned, and yet, in the face of the contention of the Auditor

General, backed by legal opinion sustaining his position, the kon. Minister of Railways and Canals still persists in asking parliament to assent to a revote of this sum of money to be paid under such circumstances. I say that this is a matter even more serious than the unsavoury case which the hon. gentleman put through in the dying hours of a session and of a parliament, and I hope the hon. gentleman will not add another outrage to the one he committed last year by asking us to vote this sum.
I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) is very choice or very apt in the language he employs.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is not a very choice case.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: All of them.

He was forced to acknowledge that he was wrong in his opinion in regard to most of them, but he adhered to his opinion as regards this. He paid the others, and he did not pay this. I say that when parliament has passed an appropriation, parliament is supreme, and a vote by parliament ought to be sufficient to satisfy even the Auditor General of this Dominion, and the gentlemen that he has associated with him. Unless the committee desires, I shall not go into the particulars which make up this claim. It is sufficient, I think, to state that the matter was gone into most fully and minutely last year. Gentlemen opposite presented the strongest arguments against this claim, but parliament voted the appropriation, and it was the business and the duty of the Auditor General to issue the cheques for that amount, when parliament declared itself satisfied upon the question. I think it would be beneath the dignity of parliament for us now to make any explanations to the Auditor General as to

why we voted last year an amount which we had a perfect right to vote, in the exercise of our discretion as a parliament.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not going into a history of this claim, hut, it is fresh in the minds of the gentlemen who sat here last year, that an agreement was come to, that a full settlement was made with the Gilbert Bros., and that afterwards the Gilbert Bros, and their solicitor resurrected an old claim, and got the minister to sanction it.

The claim was brought in the very moment it was settled what damages should be allowed for the cutting short in respect of the work which was to be done, and which was not done, leaving open the question of past claims. This claim was brought in instantly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The solicitor for Mr. Gilbert very adroitly drew up a receipt to the department, and it was understood to be for a settlement in full, without any reservation whatever. I am not reflecting on the legal profession in the least, but, this was a lawyer's receipt, and the gentleman who drew up that receipt, with a skill that only belongs to the legal profession, came back afterwards and said that the receipt might be read in two ways, and that the Gilbert Bros, might have a further claim. I challenge the minister to say that this was not included in the other items.
No, Sir, it was not. I say unhesitatingly that it was not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister will find many, if not the whole, of the items of the same kind and character included.
Not at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Not at all.

Let the minister consult the records of the past, and he will find that what I am saying is correct. The Minister of Railways has told us, in so many words, that the Auditor General is a menace to him, and that government in this country is intolerable with the Auditor General. According to the minister we should dispense with the Auditor General, because he avails of every pretext to stand in the way of the government.
Blocked the payment of moneys that were justly due.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Whether there is a Liberal or Conservative government in power, it is the duty of the Auditor General to look after the expenditures. That is what the Auditor General is there for. I venture to say that the Conservative party had the same trouble with the Auditor General, and I believe it was in the interest of the coun-

try that the Conservative government had the same trouble with him that the Liberal government has to-day. It is no excuse to say that parliament voted this money. Parliament voted that money very improperly, and it voted it when only a fraction of the representatives of the people were present in the House, and the minister left over the vote for an occasion of that kind. I am not going to say that he has done the isame thing to-day, but I want to tell the minister that the people of the country will attach considerable importance to the contentions of the Auditor General and of Mr. Lash. The minister says he does not know what the standing of Mr. Lash is.
I did not say that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I can say to the minister that Mr. Lash is considered to be a good lawyer, and was once Deputy Minister of Justice. The minister told us that he did not know what the status of Mr. Lash is.
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister told us that Mr. Lash was wrong. I am not going to say whether Mr. Lash was right or wrong, because I do not know anything about it. But, we have the fact that this was understood by the department to be a full settlement. I feel it my duty to protest against the government of the day taking the course they have taken with regard to this claim. It is a grave matter, not so much measured by the sum being asked, but when we open the doors to that sort of thing, both sides of the House can see how easily unsavoury claims of this kind can be put through, notwithstanding the opposition of the Auditor General, backed up by one of the best legal authorities in the province of Ontario.

I have a personal knowledge of the matter for which the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has been attacked-a knowledge which, I think, justifies me in laying before the House the facts as I understand them. The hon. member for Bothwell has not made a strong case ; and if it were not for the very strong language he has used, talking about jobs and indecency, it would not be necessary for me to refer to the matter at any length. I cannot understand what he means by indecency.
Was not the hon. gentleman himself the solicitor of the company in this matter ?

Then that would probably enable me to speak of the case with a good deal more knowledge than the hon. member for Bothwell. I am going to speak of something I know about, whereas the hon. gentleman has been speaking of something he knows nothing at all about. If

the hon. member wishes to say beforehand that anything I may say is not worthy of being listened to simply because I am a member of the firm who acted as solicitors for these gentlemen, I would like to understand if that is the position he takes. The hon. gentleman speaks of indecency. I do not know that it is indecent for the hon. Minister of Railways to submit something to parliament simply because the Auditor General has objected to it.
I did not make use of the word ' indecency,' though it was repeated time and again by the hon. Minister of Railways.

I heard the word ' indecent ' ; if the hon. gentleman takes it back, that settles it. The hon. gentleman also spoke of a job. Is it to he called a job because parliament is asked to vote this item after the Auditor General has pronounced against it ? Is not parliament the proper authority ? Is it not superior to the Auditor General ? If the Auditor General, by his numerous and interminable objections, has prevented this claim being paid, what is the Minister of Railways to do but bjri'ng it down to the House and have it revoted ? If the hon. gentleman will only take up the papers and give fifteen minutes to the case, he will be constrained to take back everything he has said as to this being a job. These contractors, as far back as 1893, not under the Liberal government, but under the Conservative government, filed claims in the department under three different heads : first, extras ; second, work done ; and third, a percentage for loss of profits on works which had been abandoned. The hon. gentleman has confounded the claim for work done with the claim on account of loss of profits on abandoned works. The late government dealt exclusively with the claim for loss of profits on abandoned works, and paid $29,500, or 15 per cent on $195,000, on that account; and the receipt wlas prepared, not by the lawyers of the Gilbert Company, but by the Department of Justice ; and the receipt which the member for Bothwell referred to specially reserved from that settlement the very item which is now being revoted. The letter to which my hon. friend has referred is the letter of the solicitor, Mr. Ferguson, accepting the payment of the $29,500 in the same terms as were contained in the receipt prepared in the Department of Justice. These two claims are entirely different. The claim for loss of profits on abandoned work was settled in the manner stated in 1893. At that time this claim among others was before the minister, but was not settled. In 1896 or 1897 the Gilbert Company urged these claims. There were thirteen items, of which five or six were refused. Nine items were tvotied by this parliament, and every one of these items was objected to in the Auditor General's office, and the Auditor General
sent his officers to Cornwall, where they examined every officer on the canai, and the solicitors for the Gilbert Company had to appear before the Auditor General on as many as twenty-five or thirty occasions. Every item was fought, and the Auditor General yielded every one of those items except this one ; and he gives the opinion of Mr. Lash. Now, Mr. Lash gave an opinion entirely different to the position taken by the Auditor General. I have the greatest respect for Mr. Lash, but the opinion he gave was based on an ex parte statement prepared by the Auditor General, a very one-sided statement.
It was prepared by Mr. Hayter.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Probably it was Mr. Hayter. I do not think the Auditor General himself knew anything about it. What does Mr. Lash find ? That the contractors are not entitled to be paid $10,500 for the old stone in the culvert, because it formed part of the 15 per cent allowed to them for the loss of profits on abandoned works. That is absolutely untrue ; it is against all the facts. What were the facts with reference to this old stone ? I think it is the clearest case of all the items in these claims. By the contract and the specifications the contractors bound themselves to remove an old culvert which was in the channel, and which would be too high because of the increased depth of the channel. They were to be paid for removing it, and, as part of the price, they were to be given the stone in the old culvert. There were 3,000 yards of that stone. The government did not allow them to take the culvert away, and gave it to somebody else ; and these contractors, in order to carry on their work, had to go and buy 3,000 yards of stone from other people. That is the claim before the House, which the hon. member for Bothwell calls a job. If the hon. member 'will only read the report of the resident engineer, Mr. Rubidge, which he will find at page A-37 of the Auditor General's report, he will find that this claim is for payment to these people for stone which became their property on the day they signed the contract, and of which it is shown by the clearest possible evidence they were deprived. The stone was valued at one time at $4 per yard, but the resident engineer refused to allow more than $3.50. This item, after being investigated in the department by the chief engineer, and after the House had passed on it and ordered it to be paid, was again investigated in the office of the Auditor General from time to time and payment refused. The hon. member for Bothwell is speaking altogether of something which he is totally ignorant of.

The hon. gentleman himself does not seem to understand the question, although I believe he was the

party who got the claim and pressed it before the Department of Railways and Canals. What are the facts ? In the settlement of 1894, Gilbert Bros, were to get 15 per cent allowance for the abandoned work.
On what ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: On the total amount. But if the contention of the hon. member (Mr. Belcourt) is right, namely, that this stone taken from the culvert could be used for the purposes of construction in the new work to be finished, why were the contractors made an allowance of 15 per cent on the whole work ? They are allowed a profit, as if the stone were put into the work. Are you going to pay them over again? The hon. gentleman is not right when he says that this stone which was taken out of the culvert could be used for the purposes of the new work. The contractor was allowed for the abandonment of that work altogether 15 per cent on the whole of it. Are those not the facts ?
No.

Well, I am glad to see that both Mr. Lash and the Auditor General agree with me. Here is what Mr. Lash Bays :
It appears from the papers that included in the works not proceeded with there was a quantity of masonry for which the stone in the culvert, had it been removed, might have been used. Assuming that this stone would have been so used had the work been proceeded with, it is clear that the use of this stone would have entered into the question of [DOT] the amount of profits which the contractor would have made in the execution of this work. These profits, by agreement of 'die parties, were fixed at 15 per cent of the estimated cost, and in this way it seems clear to me that the payment made in 1894 covered any claim of the contractors for not being allowed to use this stone.
So that the opinion of Mr. Lash agrees thoroughly with that of the Auditor General, and is in accord with common sense. There is not the slightest doubt that in the allowance made by the government in the settlement of 1894, these parties receivd 15 per cent of the contract which was abandoned, to cover all this work. They have been paid in full. The only question remaining is the payment of this stone. That stone was in the culvert belonging to the government, which the contractors had to take down, and which they said they could utilize in the new work. They never would have been allowed to so utilize it. They would have been obliged to use it for backing and throwing over the bank of the canal altogether. Independent of the technicality of the claim, the statement that the contractors intended to use the stone for the construction of the new work, is a false statement, I have no hesitation in saying. No stone in any culvert was used for any of the purposes of the new work. It is a trumped up claim, but independently of that here is the Mr. HAGGART.
opinion of Mr. Lash that, under the bargain of 1894, the contractors were paid in full.
The Auditor General submitted the question to Mr. Lash, and Mr. Lash agreed with him, that the contractors had no claim whatever, legally or otherwise, and we are now asked to look into this trumped up claim and vote a sum which the Auditor General refused to pay.
I would be much obliged to my hon. friend if he could point out where the Auditor General took the ground that this claim was settled in the arrangement of 1894.
I take Mr. Lash's statement in reply to Mr. McDougall. The Auditor General took two grounds, one of which was that the claim was included in the settlement of 1S94.
He never took that ground.

That is what Mr. Lash says, but I affirm that up to the time Mr. McDougall wrote that letter, he never took that ground. The ground which he took was that it was not shown in evidence that these contractors could have used this stone in other parts of the work. He did not take the ground that it was included in the settlement of 1894.

I think that the Minister of Railways and Canals used rather strong language about the Auditor General in connection with this matter, when he described the objection raised by the Auditor General as a frivolous one, and used a great many more adjectives of a similar character. I do not suppose it possible for any one to thoroughly understand the question in a few minutes, but I have read Mr. Lash's opinion, and it seems to me not only logical, but according to common sense. The hon. member for Ottawa says that the stone became the property of the contractors. I do not see how that pretension can be sustained.

Would the hon. gentleman allow me ? I -would like to point out to him the exact wording of the clause of the specification which treats of this stone as the property of the contractor. It will be found on page A-36 of the Auditor General's Report, iu Mr. Rubidge's letter. Mr. Rubidge says :
By the terms of the contract the stone and these culverts became the property of the contractors.

That is referred to t>y Air. Rubidge in his letter, on page A-36.	The stone in the culvert is said, by the terms of the specifications, to become the property of the contractor.
By the terms of the contract the stone in these culverts became the property of the contractors, as clearly indicated by the special provision that they (the contractors) should provide at their own expanse piling ground for the stone. If the stone was intended to remain the property of the government, ' spoil ground ' or ' piling ground ' would have been provided at the government's expense. The provisions of the contract made all the stone in these culverts the property of the contractors. The approximate quantities furnished by the government placed the amount at 3,000 yards, and in consequence contractors' claim was limited to this amount. A condition in the contract provided that the canal would be unwatered to allow the stone in culverts to be removed. The government's failure to conform to this provision deprived the contractors of obtaining possession and use of the stone.
These are the exact facts.
Has the hon. gentleman been reading the contract ?
No, I am quoting from the resident engineer.

1 am not much concerned about what Air. Rubidge said. AVhat I want is the terms of the contract. I find that the contract is referred to by Air. Lash, and I suppose he had it before him at the time, provided that the contractor had the right to use stone, the property of the government, in building a certain work for the government. How the hon. gentleman can say that, under these circumstances, the stone became the property of the contractor, I do not understand. I do not see how the hon. gentleman can venture to make such an assertion. The stone was always the property of the government. Aly hon. friend wants the House to believe that this stone became the property of the contractor.
Certainly.

Why, it is not arguable. Mr. Lash is perfectly correct in the view he took of it. But, whether Mr. Lash is right or wrong is one question, and whether the Auditor General should be referred to as he has been referred to by the Minister of Railways and Canals is another question. I venture to think that when an Auditor General refers any matter of this kind to a counsel of the standing of Mr. Lash and is supported in his view by that counsel, it does not become the Alinister of Railways and Canals or any other member of the government to rise in this House and make such accusations against the Auditor General as the hon. gentleman has made today.

What accusation ? I say that
the Auditor General undertook to override the action of the parliament and to assume control over this parliament-and I must repeat it. Parliament voted this money with full and satisfactory knowledge of the case, and that ought to be enough to satisfy ten thousand auditor generals.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We will deal with one Auditor General at a time. What I venture to suggest to the hon. gentleman is that, dealing with one Auditor General and one counsel, we find that that Auditor General is supported in his contention by a counsel of the highest possible standing in Canada. Under these circumstances, it does not become the hon. gentleman or any member of the government to speak of the Auditor General's action as frivolous. I do not see any opinion of the Department of Justice, but I do see an opinion presented by the law clerk of the Department of Railways and Canals.
Alay I ask the hon. gentleman a question ? Is it his opinion that the Auditor General ought to sit in judgment on the doings of this House ? That, I think, is a fair question ?

The suggestion that I was making was that the action of the Auditor General did not deserve the terms applied to it by the Minister of Railways and Canals. The Auditor General found a difficulty in authorizing the payment of this money and sought the opinion of an eminent counsel of the same bar as that of which the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton) is a member, and that counsel supported him in' his view. Under the circumstances, his conduct ought not to be characterized as it has been characterized by the Minister of Railways and Canals. As I say, I do not find an opinion from the Department of Justice, but I do find an opinion of the law clerk of the Department of Railways and Canals which says :
I find it difficult to follow Mr. Lash's reasoning.
I do not find much difficulty of that kind myself.
It seems to me that dealing with the question reasonably and practically, without legal refinements, no such conclusion can be arrived at.
I do not know what this gentleman means by 'legal refinements.' I suppose that Air. Lash was dealing with the question from a legal standpoint, and, dealing with it from a legal standpoint, he dealt with it in a way in which it seems to be impossible to arrive at a different conclusion.
What is the hon. gentleman reading from ?

From a memorandum from the law clerk of the Department of Railways and Canals at page A-51. Further than that, he says :

It is true, that speaking with legal technicality the actual property in or ownership of the stone would not pass to the contractors-
So my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Bel-court) does not agree with

x
If the hon. gentleman will read on, he will find that the law clerk agrees with me.

I will read on :
-but the clear intention of the parties was that the contractors could use this stone in the work; in other words, that the government would provide a certain quantity of stone.

Yes, and he says :
The true measure of the contractor's claim, in my view, is the cost of the stone, which the contractors had to supply to replace the stone which the government failed, contrary to the provision in the specification, to allow them to use. In an action for damages at law for breach of a similar contract between two individuals, the test I have mentioned would be the measure of damages for the breach and the burden of proof would be on the party making default.

I do not know what my hon. friend's opinion is. He is speaking, I suppose, from the standpoint of the contractor. ' I am speaking from the standpoint of the interest of the country, and I say that, so far as the property in this stone is concerned, it is perfectly clear that the law clerk of the Department of Railways agrees with Mr. Lash. As to the question whether or not that is covered by the terms of the receipt which was given, they do not agree. Mr. Lash thought the terms of the receipt precluded any payment being made on this account. For my part, with the little attention I have been able to give to the matter, I would be disposed to agree with Mr. Lash. I see nothing 5" the memorandum of the law clerk to lead me to a different conclusion. But, as I say, that is not the particular matter I rose to discuss. I thought it my duty to say a word on behalf of the Auditor General, in view of the language the hon. minister had used.

Is the Gilbert Dredging Company still employed at $425 a day ? I notice that in 1898 they received $72,6-4G; in 1899, $103,734 ; and in 1900, $123,772, or a total of $300,152. Are they still engaged in this profitable job ?

They have done nothing this year. That was the tail end of an old arrangement that had been made by my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) and those associated with him.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
One of the astounding things is the connection of the hon. member for Ottawa with the case. Are the House and the country to understand that when claims are being brought before the Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
different departments, claimants must necessarily appeal to a member of parliament to steer their claims through ?
This claim was made by Mr. Ferguson, who was at one time member of the Conservative Association in Ottawa..
So long as Mr. Ferguson was engaged in the matter, there was no fault to be found, because he was not a member of parliament
Nor was I at this time. I was associated with Mr. Ferguson in this case as far back as in 1893, long before I entered parliament.

Then I submit the hon. gentleman should have seen the propriety of withdrawing from this case, or from presenting any claim against the government since he became a member of parliament. Now, what position is the Auditor General placed in ? He is between two fires. On one side he has the minister, on the other side he has the member for Ottawa. Listen to this report.
But what about parliament to which this matter must be submitted and voted on ?

Here is the part of the correspondence which shows the extremity to which the Auditor General is driven. He says :
I notice in the correspondence a letter from Mr. Belcourt in which he speak3 of my ' interminable objections.' I wonder whether it is possible to find any person in my position, with some conscience, who is so amiable that he would throw away over $10,000 of public money for fear of wounding the feeling of claimants or their solicitors, by raising an objection to such a proposal as Mr. Belcourt supported in the interests of the Gilbert Blasting Company.
Now, Sir, the House might as well understand that this is the position of matters to-day. Where a claitn of a dubious nature has to be fathered, the assistance has to be sought of a member of this House as solicitor. It is a notorious fact that in the last parliament correspondence was lying on this side of the House which implicated six members of parliament, for a consideration of $1,500, in supporting a certain railway Bill in this House. It is a notorious fact that such was the case. I myself saw copies of the correspondence, and it was only when the parties refunded the money that the actual receipts were handed back to them. Now, Sir, I submit that if a member of parliament, a member of this House, is to be licensed, and members of the government are to condone such grievous faults
Where is the fault ?
Why, the hon. gentleman seems lost to a sense of what is the duty of members of parliament.
Will the hon. member allow me to ask him a question ? Does1 he mean to say that because I became a member of this House I must cease practising my profession ? Is that what he means ?

No, but I submit that the hon. member, or any other gentleman who is a member of this House, has no right to take claims before ministers of the Crown when he is a supporter of the government. If the hon. gentleman was an opponent of the government, then so much could not be said against it. But even under those circumstances, it would not be In the best taste. But when the hon. gentleman is a supporter of the government, then I say it is grossly wrong, and the hon. ' gentleman has no more right to appear in that capacity before the department than he has a right to go up to the Railway Committee and openly advocate a Bill that he has before that committee. If the hon. gentleman has a right to go there and carry with him his vote and his voice, then I submit that twenty members of this House have a right to go into that committee and vote for the consideration that is given to them, just in the same way that counsel may be paid a consideration for appearing before the committee.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me ? Is the hon. gentleman aware
Six o'clock.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that a solicitor cannot appear for the Crown, cannot act for the Crown, that the statute prohibits his doing so ?

No, I am not.
At six o'clock, committee book recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Department of Railways and Canals-To provide for the appointment of S. L. T. McKnight to a junior second-class clerkship, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $700.
What is the necessity of taking a person outside of those who have passed the Civil Service Act V Who is this Mr. McKnight ?
He is in the department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How long has he been in the department ?
For three or four years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has he any special qualifications that would require him to be appointed notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act ?

He is not in the regular civil service, but he is in the extra service. He has passed his examination, but he cannot get his salary and come in as a junior second-class clerk under the legislation passed last year without having this provision added.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: He can come in at the minimum salary.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: He has been three years in the department ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And you think he is entitled to $700 ?

Yes.
Intercolonial Railway, $4,100,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What are you going to do with this-build a new railway ? Could the hon. minister give us some information as to what this is wanted for ?

I have been delaying with the expectation that my hon. friend (Mr. Hag-gart), who has been more particularly giving attention to this subject, would implement the statement that he made the other iday in the House. I do no say that he actually alarmed me, but he made the declaration that he intended to attack the general policy, administration and management of the Intercolonial Railway by moving, when Mr. Speaker would leave the Chair, a motion on the subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes.

And that he Intended to precipitate a full dress debate in respect to it. Under these alarming circumstances, I have thought that my hon. friend would naturally expect that he would be looked to to take the initiative in the matter, and would precipitate this full dress debate which he declared he would bring on. I have been waiting to hear what he had to say in reference to the management of the Intercolonial Railway, and to hear what it might be well, perhaps, that I should remark upon when we came to discuss this item. Do I understand my hon. friend does not desire to avail himself of the opportunity of doing that ? If he does not, I wall proceed to make any statement that I have to make upon this subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister has, perhaps, misunderstood what I intended to say. I intend to move a motion. I think, the day after to-morrow, on going into supply, upon this question ; so, that he may proceed with his estimate.
