Then, the hon. gentleman, I

presume, would contemplate a general debate upon the question of the management of the Intercolonial Railway ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes.
If so, I suppose it will hardly be worth while haying two debates on the subject ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No.
And in that case it may be better to go on ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There are just a few remarks to be made on the item which is going through. It was my intention, and I think it is my intention, to propose an amendment, and the day after to-morrow I will be prepared, on the motion to go into supply, to move an amendment, and we can debate the motion.

The hon. Minister of Railways will remember that early in the session a question was asked by the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) relative to the purchase of certain lands for the purpose of enlarging the grounds of the Intercolonial Railway at Lfivis, and that an answer was given. Will the hon. minister state the position of those expropriated lands whether the same have been paid for, and if so, the rates that have been paid.

There has been no change whatever in the situation from that which existed the other day when the subject was up. No progress has been made. The matter remains in statuo quo. The same lands which were unsettled and unpaid for then are unsettled and unpaid for now. The same intention, which I declared was in my mind in regard to the expropriation of these lands, continues and exists down to the present moment, so that there is actually no alteration in the situation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In connection with the matter of increased accommodation at L6vis for the purposes of the Intercolonial Railway, I wish to refer to certain correspondence which has been laid on the Table of the House. From this correspondence it would appear that as far back as 1S9S, the Department of Railways and Canals contemplated the purchase of some additional land in that town. In that connection, I understand from the correspondence that Mr. Jones, a trusted and well-known employee of the Department of Railways and Canals, was commissioned by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to proceed to Levis to make inquiries. After going there, and after his return to Ottawa, Mr. Jones made a report to the minister, and perhaps I had better read portions of that report. The officer to whom was entrusted this work says :

Memo, for the Hon. A. G. Blair :
By your instructions I visited LSvis on the 28th November, 1898, in connection with the expropriation of land for the increased accommodation at LSvis station; but before doing so,
I had an interview that morning with the Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick in Quebec. Dr. Howlin accompanied me to Ldvis. I called upon each of the land-owners and saw them personally with the following results :

Then, he has given a statement as to the parties that he called on. and as to the value they put upon their land ;

Young, 95 cents per square foot.
Gilbert Carriere, $1.22 per square foot.
Edouard Couture, $1.36 per square foot.
The estate of Rhodes, $1 per square foot.
Unfilled land. 50 cents per square foot.
Furthermore, to the report, Mr. Jones adds the following clause ;
I saw Mr. Fitzpatrick on my return, who thought all these prices too high; but they are the very lowest that the owners would consent to name to me. (Sgd.) L. K. Jones, Secretary.
It is apparent from that letter, that on the 1st of December, 1898, these parties placed values upon their property, ranging from 95 cents to $1.36 per foot. It will be noticed that Mr. Fitzpatrick, the Solicitor General, stated to Mr. Jones that he considered this price too high. I have no doubt that the Minister of Railways, in view of the statement made by Mr. Jones, saw Mr. Fitzpatrick in regard to the matter, because it was rather important, involving as it did an expenditure of over $100,000. I assume that there were interviews between the Minister of Railways and the Solicitor General, because the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) was convinced that these prices were altogether too high, and he subsequently endorsed on the statement a memo, to this effect :
Offer 80 cents per foot for the filled land and 40 cents for the unfilled. (Sgd.) A. G'. Blair.
There cannot be a doubt that the minister arrived at that conclusion after hearing the representations not only of Mr. Fitzpatrick, but of his officer, Mr. Jones. Nothing seems to have been done for some little time, and we find from the correspondence that in the month of May following, the minister without portfolio (Hon. Mr. Dobell) was asked by the Minister of Railways to look after the purchasing of these lands. On the 17th of May, 1900, Mr. Dobell wrote from the city of Quebec ;
I only want to call your attention to the fact that there are one or two things not definitely settled about Levis. You have closed with Young, and you have given me authority to offer Couture $1 a foot for two lots; about 20,000 feet north and south of the depot, as marked on your plan. I have done this, and have added further that he gives us the option until the 1st of July next of taking the remainder of the property by buying the additional 20,000, and I do not hesitate to strongly advise you to do this. >
It will be noticed that on the date of this letter the lands that were acquired by the Department of Railways had received different valuations. Mr. Jones had reported that he thought the prices of from 90 cents to $1.36 per foot were too high, and Mr. Fitzpatrick endorsed that opinion. So firmly convinced was the minister that this price was too high, that he endorsed on the memo, that in his opinion SO cents a foot was a fair price. According to the letter of Mr. Dobell, one of the largest vendors of the property, namely, Mr. Couture, was prepared to sell his land for $1 per foot. It is well that the House should bear the two dates in mind, namely, December, '98, and the 17th of May, 1899. The matter seems to have hung fire for a considerable time despite the fact that there was a standing offer up to July, 1900, to sell at $1 per foot. The correspondence goes on and nothing seems to have been done by the minister during the year 1900 ; the minister not seeing fit to avail of the standing offer of Mr. Couture to buy at $1 per foot-and I will deal only with the offer of Mr. Couture for the present. We find that on the 15th of March, 1901, other gentlemen intervened on behalf of Mr. Couture. At first Mr. Couture appears to have been working personally in the matter, or through Mr. Lemieux, a notary, and Mr. Lemieux had impressed upon the government the necessity of closing the sale, as appears by the correspondence. Mr. Couture not being taken at his offer, of $1 per foot, we find that about March 15, 1901, Mr. Couture had secured the services of Mr. Prefontaine, the member for Maisonneuve, or the law firm with which he is connected. It is rather peculiar that this gentleman in the city of Quebec who offered land to the department at $1 a foot, secures the services, six months after, of a member of this House, and through the law firm of which he is a partner, makes a demand of the government in regard to the price of these lands. And, Sir, the lands that the department refused to1 pay $1 a foot for, they afterwards purchased at $1.50 a foot. As the purchase amounted to upwards of $100,060, it will be seen what difference that will make. When Mr. Couture acquired these new legal advisers, he withdrew his offer of $1 per foot, and lo and behold you, not only has he secured the assistance of a member of parliament to press his claim, but a gentleman from a very far distance away is brought into the transaction also. On the 15th of March application is made through the firm of Prefontaine, Archer & Co., of Montreal, to sell the lands at the enhanced price of $2.50 per foot, although these same lands were offered at $1 a foot a few months before. This afternoon I complained about a solicitor being a member of this House and taking upon himself the duty of furthering claims before any department of the government. As it
was in the case of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt), so it is with the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Prefontaine), and in my opinion he should be blamed for coming before the department and endeavouring to press a claim of this kind before the minister. It does not look well for the Department of Railways and Canals that that department should have taken the action it did after this gentleman at Quebec had secured the services of a Montreal member of this parliament, who is a power behind this government, and whose name is always put prominently forward as being about to enter the cabinet. But Mr. Couture was not satisfied at retaining the services of a firm in Montreal, and he appears to have gone to the city of St. John, N.B., to enlist the sympathy and assistance of a gentleman who is very near and very dear, politically and personally, to the Minister of Railways and Canals. I find on file the following letter, dated the 15th of March, 1901 :
Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your communication of the 1st inst., relative to the property of Mr. L. E. Couture, situated at Levis, P.Q., on the line of the Intercolonial Railway, by which you state, if the matter could he settled immediately, you are of opinion that you could induce Mr. G. Archer, solicitor, Montreal, to get his client to accept the sum of $2.25 per foot for the property in question. In reply, I am, by direction, to inform you that the department cannot entertain the settlement of this matter on any such terms.
The letter to which this is a reply is a letter addressed by Mr. Pugsley to the department, as follows :
Fredericton, N.B., March 1, 1901. Hon. A. G. Blair,
Minister of Railways and Canals,
Ottawa.
Re Couture Property, Levis..
My dear Blair,-Mr. Charles Archer, of Montreal, has sent me copies of solemn declaration of L. M. CarriSre, M.P., &c.
After carefully reading the declarations, it seems to me that a very strong case is made for a valuation of at least $2.50 a foot. If the matter could he settled immediately, I can, I feel sure, induce Mr. Archer to get his clients to accept $2.25. I will esteem it a great favour if you will kindly take the matter up, and settle upon this basis.
Yours sincerely,

Mr. Pugsley, not being a member of this House or connected in any way with the legislation of this parliament, has a perfect right to act as solicitor for any party who applies for his services in the furtherance of a claim against the department; hut the hon. member for Maisonneuve and his firm are estoped by all the rules of propriety from acting in such a matter. Now, what are the facts in this case ? Here was a man coming to the department and offering his land at $1 a foot. Here was a member of the cabinet saying that he believed $1 a

foot was a fair price. Here was the minister himself, prior to that time, on the evidence adduced before him. and on the advice of the Solicitor General, refusing to give $1 a foot-why ? Because he had heard Mr. Fitzpatrick's opinion and he had the evidence of his own official to the contrary. And afterwards Mr. Couture through his solicitor makes the claim of $2.50 a foot. My sympathy goes with the Minister of Railways and Canals, for I believe he was desirous of acquiring this land at $1 a foot, and if he had had his own way he would have acquired it at that price, and the deal would have been closed and the country no doubt saved a large amount of money. But when the minister has formulated his policy, the lion, member for Maisonneuve comes forward with his high proposition, and Mr. Pugsley supports it. Mr. Pugsley has a perfect right to do so ; but at the same time it is a reflection on the head of the Department of Railways and Canals that, by reason of the great intimacy political and personal that exists between the minister and Mr. Pugsley, parties in the city of Quebec feel that if they wish to prosecute a claim in that department to the best possible advantage, they must go to the city of St. John and secure the services of Mr. Pugsley. A little while ago the minister gave an answer to a question to the effect that Mr. Couture had withdrawn his offer of $1 a foot, and that he was now demanding $2.50 a foot. So that the minister is in this dilemma, that he cannot close on the original offer of $1 a foot, and now the matter is going or has gone in the Exchequer Court. While the minister was endeavouring to hew to the line and to make the best possible deal for the country, the Solicitor General was interfering and advising the department against the acceptance of the offer of $1 a foot as being too high. But later on, when the price demanded is $2.50 a foot, the Solicitor General writes to Mr. Schreiber, the deputy of the department, the following letter :
Ottawa, 29th March, 1901.
Dear Mr. Schreiber,-X beg to inclose herewith a copy of a letter received from Mr. Lemieux, the agent at Levis, with reference to the expropriation of land required there for station ground. The prices fixed for the property of Couture and Turgeon are, X think, under the circumstances, reasonable, and our agent at LSvis, Mr. Lemieux, writes another letter yesterday to say that if the matter is not concluded within eight days from yesterday Couture may withdraw his offer- I send you copies of both letters.
Yours truly,

I was ill error when X stated that Mr. Fitzpatrick was recommending the payment of $2.50, the fact being that he- was at that time recommending the payment of $1.50, although only two months before he had stated openly to an official of the department that he believed $1 a foot was too high. But

while the minister was being pressed by gentlemen who had seats in this House, and by his personal and political friend Mr. Pugsley, and also by the Solicitor General, to pay this enhanced price, there was another gentleman pressing the same thing upon him, and that was no less a person than the Prime Minister himself; because I find that on the 19th of March, 1901, the following letter is addressed to Mr. Schreiber, the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals :
Quebec, 19th March, 1900. Collingwood Schreiber, Esq.,
Deputy Minister Railways and Canals, Ottawa.
My dear Sir,-On receipt of your message here to-day, I immediately wired you as follows: -
' Please advise me as to nature of report you require re Ldvis.'
I am prepared to make such a report as you may require in order to facilitate this matter, but in the meantime I can say that the titles have been examined and found in order, and the Prime Minister is convinced that the remuneration asked is reasonable.
So far as regards the necessity of making any purchases is concerned, this is a matter of which I know absolutely nothing.
Yours truly,

Now, Sir, what is the position ? First, the minister was having forced on him land at $1 a foot. Whether he was endeavouring to carry out the deal on that basis or not X know not; but I know this, that the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General were both endeavouring to force him to pay $1.50 a foot for land which had been offered to the department for $1. Whether the Prime Minister was responsible for this recommendation or not, I know not; but it can hardly be believed that Mr. Fitzpatrick would use his name in this matter unless he had full leave and license to do so. It would be bad enough if the department were forced to pay $1.50 a foot for this land. Mr. Couture has done what any man under reasonable circumstances would do: he has refused to accept even the $1.50, and today there is hanging up in the Department of Railways and Canals a claim for this land at $2.50 a foot. Everybody has heard the statement made by, the Prime Minister throughout the province of Ontario as to the Intercolonial Railway. He said : ' What did we find when we got into power ? We found the Intercolonial commencing nowhere and ending nowhere-ending in a field near the city of Quebec.' And yet these gentlemen are demanding to-day the price of $120,000 per acre for these very lands. The whole matter bears on its face evidence that there is a political deal and a job, and the Minister of Railways is to be blamed for this, that he did not close at $1 a foot when the lands were offered to him at that figure. The minister is to be sympathized with for having yielded to the appeal of the First Minister and the Solicitor

Genera] to pay enhanced prices. Everybody knows what a trial in the Exchequer Court means. The strongest evidence possible will be forthcoming on behalf of the claimants, and in view of the valution made by the Solicitor General, it is easily seen what the outcome will be; and when next session comes round, no doubt a large appropriation will be asked for to pay for these lands, and the country will be forced to pay, not $1 per foot, but $2.50 per foot.
So much for the one case. Let us turn now to another one, known as the Rhodes case. There seem to have been several different properties in that estate, and a gentleman named Dr. Howlin, representative of the Rhodes estate, made an offer of soqie of them. In his report Mr. Jones says that Dr. Howlin offered the filled land at $1 a foot and the unfilled at 50 cents a foot. Afterwards Mr. Campbell, who, I presume, is *a real estate agent in Quebec, said the estate was anxious to close out the sale at $1 a foot. In the meantime the minister reported that the land was not worth $1 a foot, but 80 cents, but in that case, as in the last, there appeared on the scene a very powerful friend of the government, and a gentleman who had a perfect right to go before the department inasmuch as he was not a member of this House. But I will be bound to say that the services of that gentleman were sought by reason of the fact that he was supposed to have, as no doubt he has, a very vast influence on this government-I will not say particularly on the Department of Railways and Canals, but on all the departments. That gentleman is the Hon. Charles Langelier. Hon. gentlemen opposite smile as if Mr. Langelier had no influence with the government. True, the Toronto Globe said some years ago that he ought to be in jail, but he has a vast amount of influence with this government, and no doubt that is the reason why he intervened on behalf of this estate. What is the position of the Rhodes estate ? That property which was offered at $1 a foot, and for which the minister was willing to pay 80 cents, is being hung up at the price of $2.50 per foot, and in a very pathetic letter Mi-. Langelier said :
3rd May, 1900.
My dear Blair,-I have the honour to forward you the resolution which.the town of LSvis is ready to pass if the government accept the condition therein contained. I need not tell you how I would like to have this bargain carried through.

What land is the hon. gentleman speaking of ? The land that was originally offered by Dr. Howlin at $1 a foot and for which I offered 80 cents a foot, was sold by Dr. Howlin on behalf of the Rhodes estate and purchased by the government at 80 cents a foot.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Of course I stand corrected as to the Rhodes property.
We bought from the Rhodes estate at 80 cents.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That does not take away from the fact that it is thoroughly appreciated in the city of Quebec that when a claim is to be pressed in any department of the public service, it is very advisable to secure the services of Mr. Pugsley and Mr. Langelier. Let me read from a very pathetic letter written by Mr. Langelier on the 31st of May, 1900. In this letter he says :
I do not suspect Dr. Howlin of intending to defraud, but security is the best policy in such matters. Once again, I ask the favour of protecting me for my fees. The moment the amount is paid, the doctor is going to return to England, and it is better for me to have the whole thing settled before he leaves.
A fair construction to place on that letter is this. That Dr. Howlin had secured the services of this very powerful gentleman, and Mr. Langelier had a grave suspicion that the amount he might be paid would not be at all commensurate with his idea of the value of his service, and so he preferred to j have the cheque first and pay himself and I igijve the balance to Dr. Howlin, if any balance there was. There is the position, so far as Mr. Langelier is concerned.
It is due to the House and the country that the Minister of Railways and Canals should explain why he did not accept the price set by Couture of $1 a foot, or why he did not act on his own opinion that 80 cents fwas a fair price, and why, within a few months afterwards, he allowed his own opinion to be overborne and offered $1.50 per foot for the same land.
It is due to the House and the country that the Solicitor General should explain why I lie intervened and changed his opinion. It is due to the House and the First Minister that the Solicitor General should explain by what right he assured the Minister of Railways that the First Minister had declared that $1.50 was a fair price for this land. If the Minister of Railways is to be allowed his own judgment we may expect matters to go on properly. I believe that at $1 a foot the purchase would have been a judicious one. But what we are entitled to know is why the Minister of Railways should have given such an exhibition of weakness as to go back on his own opinion at the dictation of other members of the cabinet and other people with influence over the government,

While I 'do not pretenid to have any more will power ior resisting power than the average man, I cannot imagine what the hon. gentleman has in his mind when he talks of my going back upon some stand I had taken. He says that I was not willing to pay $1 a foot for a certain property but insisted that the price should be cut down to 80 cents per foot, and that then I went back on that decision. When ? Where is

the evidence that I have expressed an opinion in favour of paying a higher price ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the hon. minister will allow me to answer now, I will say that he will find in the correspondence, within a few months after, that the cheques were remitted to Quebec at the price of $1.50 a foot.

If that appears, that will be some justification for the hon. gentleman's statement. But I think he will find on reference to the papers that this was in connection with a larger purchase and not limited to this piece of land.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: For fear there should be a mistake, I would like to ask if there are two different properties of Couture ?
There are two or three properties of Couture. The whole question is in a most confused and tangled condition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has any property been purchased from Couture, and if so what price has been paid ? Because, reading the letters and examining the plan, I have found only one Couture property.
On the south side of the track, I understand, there was a piece of land purchased from Couture. I wish the hon. gentleman had intimated to me that he had intended to bring this matter up.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Mr. Couture in the correspondence says that he will not now accept $1.50 a foot, and that was the identical land that he had before offered for $1 a foot.

I do not think that is correct. I would not speak with confidence. My deputy does not remember the price paid for the Couture lot on the south side. When Mr. Jones, the secretary of the department, returned to Lfivis after looking the ground over and inquiring in the locality as to what ought to be a fair value of the lot, I offered, as the report shows, SO cents per foot for the lots then being tendered to the government. Some of the persons, the Rhodes and the Youngs, accepted the offer of 80 cents for the filled and 40 cents for the unfilled.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
On February 25th the hon. gentleman from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) asked a question concerning these purchases, and the hon minister in his answer included the following
Edouard Couture-22,356 3'100 square feet made grpund ; expropriation papers filed April 11, September 20 and October 19, 1900. Not yet settled.
So. from the information furnished! by the minister, no lands had been purchased from Couture, but they were the subject of expropriation.

That may possibly be so. But my officers were under the impression, as I am, that we did get a portion of land from Couture on the south side of the line. But I was going on to say that the Young estate and the Rhodes estate accepted the offer we made of 80 cents for filled land and 40 cents for unfilled. Mr. Couture, at that time was offering us land-not all he afterwards offered-and we concluded that we would take it if we could get it at a fair price. He would not accept an offer of 80 cents per foot, and insisted on being paid a very much higher price than even $1 a foot. He affirmed that my colleague the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dobell) was not warranted in saying that he had expressed willingness to accept even $1 a foot.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the hon. minister will allow me-he will find that the difference between the hon. member for Quebec West and Mr. Couture was that the hon. member for Quebec West stated that the price ought to be $1.40, and Mr. Couture insisted on $1.50. That was subsequent to the offer made by the hon. member for Quebec West at the rate of $1, and while this expansion process was going on aided by these gentlemen who were putting in the claims.

I have not the details of the correspondence in my mind. If the hon. gentleman intended, as no doubt he did, to bring this up, he might have intimated that such was his purpose, and in that case I could have procured all the papers and made a full statement of the facts. But I come back to this point : What does the hon. gentleman complain of ? Does he say that it is a reflection upon the government that some member of parliament may be taking up the case on behalf of either his clients or his elector and supporter? Can he say that it is a reflection on the department that a claim is made, unless he can show that it is an improper claim, and that it was allowed at an improper figure. Nothing of that kind was shown. I have been unable to satisfy myself that the price at which this land was offered for sale by any of the owners from whom we have not made a purchase was at price that we should be justified in paying. As a consequence, I have found it necessary to take legal proceedings by expropriation, and since we cannot agree upon the price to leave the price to be determined by the court. I do not know anything else that a minister can do under the circumstance. And, if the hon. gentleman now makes complaint, it must be because we did not pay over to Mr. Couture and to some of these other people the money that we were asked to pay without referring the matter to the court for adjudication. I think that is hardly sufficient ground for complaint. If we had paid the price, the

bon. gentleman would have been among the first to criticise us and to declare that we should have forced the people to prove their claim before the court.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I regret that the minister does not see the matter as I think all fair-minded men must see it, having regard to the facts of the case as they are. I will be bound to say that the evidence will not bear out the statement that we were dealing with more than one parcel of land. The minister in his answer speaks of only one parcel to be bought from Couture. We can only depend on the information that the minister gives us. If he wishes now to say that his answer was wrong, let him set it right, but let him not blame us because we were misled. And what is the evidence relating to the Couture property as it appears. The evidence shows that Mr. Jones, the minister's trusted official, went down and secured an offer of $1 a foot. The Solicitor General told Mr. Jones that the price was too high. This was in the fall of 1898. In face of the fact that Mr. Jones had stated that the lands were offered for sale for $1, and the Solicitor General has stated that that was too high a price, the minister did what might reasonably be expected, he said: I will not pay you $1, but I will pay 80 cents, if you will accept it. But what next ? It hangs fire for a few months. The hon. -member for Quebec West (Mr. Dobell) is empowered by the minister to have an interview with Couture, and he comes back with the assurance that the land is still offered for sale at the price of $1 a foot. Now, what is the next thing ? Couture at once drops out of the negotiations on his own be-~half, and he enlists the sympathy and political assistance, in addition to the assistance of the Solicitor General, of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Prefontaine). What is the next move ? The price of the land goes up from $1 to $1.50 per foot. In view of the fact that the Solicitor General had stated that $1 was too high a price to be paid for the land, within a few months the Solicitor General is recommending-whether he had fuller knowledge of the land in question or not, I know not -but he says that the lands he believed were not worth $1 are now worth $1.50. He goes further than that, as appears by the correspondence ; he states [DOT]that the premier assures him the lands are worth that. I know not whether he had authority from the premier to say so. If he had not, then he was doing that which was wrong ; and if he had authority from the premier to say so, then I say it was rather an out-of-the-way course for the premier and the Solicitor General to be pursuing to advise the minister to pay $1.50 for land that those parties had been offering at $1. What might be expected as a consequence ? Nothing could be more plain. Mr. Pugsley's services had been called into
requisition, although why in the name of all that is good, when a man has an honest claim to prosecute, he is not satisfied with the help of the most prominent members in the government, but he goes down to St. John, and. enlists the services of a strong political friend of the Minister of Railways and Canals.
Now, how much progress has he made in that business ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: He has made the progress, I presume, that he wants to make, he has got the matter into the Exchequer Court now ; and, fortified as the claim will be, with the opinion of the Solicitor General that the land is cheap at $1.50, fortified with the assistance of the opinion of the premier that the land is worth $1.50, and fortified with the assistance that lie will get from the witnesses who will no doubt be friendly to him, I won't say much as to the fight that will be put up against this contention, seeing the strong allies the claimant has. I believe that when the reports are brought down next year, and a grant of money is asked for the lands, it will be seen that Mr. Couture will receive $2, and probably more. Yet the minister sees nothing in this reprehensible. I reiterate that the minister should not have listened to the advice of his colleagues as to the value of the land. Notwithstanding the man's own offer of the land at $1.50 a foot, the minister goes outside of it, and as a result, the country has jplaced against it a claim for this land of $2.50 a foot.
What did the minister go outside of ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I regret I cannot impress upon the minister that if he had a standing offer of this land at $1-

I say to my hon. friend that the offer of $1 was not adhered to, he withdrew it, and made a further demand, a higher demand ; and as he observed a desire on our part to approach him, he raised his price still higher, and has taken steps to secure what I think is an exorbitant price for his land, which I was not willing to pay.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then, the evidence discloses this fact, that there was at one time an offer at $1 a foot, which the minister did not embrace.
Instantly, but he fell away from it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The evidence, unfortunately for the minister's contention, does not bear that out. Some three or four months elapsed and then he comes forward with his second claim for $1.50 a foot. The minister does not accept that offer. I reiterate again

tliat the minister should not have listened to the advice of the premier and to the advice of the Solicitor General as to the value of the land, when he had a standing offer of the land at $1.
His offer did not stand, it ran, and ran in a contrary direction.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No wonder it didn't stand, when he had a wink from the other eye that he was foolish to sell it at that price. Here was the minister paying $1.75 for land belonging to another friend, for the Murphy property, at least, so it is disclosed in the evidence. If the minister sees nothing wrong in the transaction, if he sees there is no exhibition of weakness on his part, if he sees there is nothing reprehensible on the part of a member of parliament coming before him and presenting a claim, if he sees nothing wrong in the whole transaction, there is one thing that he will see next session, and that the country will see, namely, that this land will have to be paid for by the Dominion of Canada at the rate of $120,000 an acre.

When I came into the House a moment ago, the hon. gentleman was saying I had made a statement that the land in question was worth $1.50 a foot. Does the hon. gentleman contend there is anything in the records to that effect 1
If the right hon. gentleman will read the correspondence, he will see a letter from Mr. Fitzpatrick, in which he said that the premier considered the price was fair. That is what I quoted.
What price ?
One dollar and fifty cents.
There is nothing of the kind in the record.
The right hon. gentleman must construe the letters together, written about that time.

There is only one letter from Mr. Fitzpatrick in the whole record here, and that reads as follows : Ottawa, 29th March, 1900.
Dear Mr. Sehreiber-I beg to inclose herewith a copy of letter received from Mr. Lemieux, the agent at Levis, with reference to the expropriation of land required there for station ground. The prices fixed for the property of Couture and Turgeon are, I think, under the circumstances, reasonable, and our agent at LSvis, Mr. Lemieux, writes another letter yesterday to say that if the matter is not concluded within eight days from yesterday, Couture may withdraw his offer. I send you copies of both letters.
Then, here is another letter dated previous to that, on the 19th of March :
On receipt of your message here to-day I immediately wired you as follows :-

' Please advise me as to nature of report you require re Levis.'
I am prepared to make such a report as you may require in order to facilitate this matter, but in the meantime I can say that the titles have been examined and found in order, and the Prime Minister is convinced that the remuneration asked is reasonable.
So far as regards the necessity of making any purchases is concerned, this is a matter of which I know absolutely nothing.
Yours truly,

Now, Mr. Speaker, that is all the correspondence I had, that is in this record, with Mr. Fitzpatrick. There is no mention of these letters of either $1, $1.50, or any price at all. I do not know what Mr. Fitzpatrick had in his mind when he wrote that way. He might have talked of the matter with me, but I knew nothing of the value of the land. Whatever may be my merits, I am no expert in the value of real estate. I know nothing at all of this property, except having passed over it in the cars. I do not know exactly where it is. Certainly, the hon. gentleman is not justified, from anything there is in this letter of iMr. Fitzpatrick, in saying that I had given my opinion that this land was worth $1 or $1.50 or any price at all. The hon. gentleman cannot show from these letters what was the value which Mr. Fitzpatrick had in his mind, or what was the value I had in my own mind-if I discussed the matter with him at all. If the Solicitor General were here himself, he could speak as to what he meant in his letter. But so far as I can see from this record, the hon. gentleman has no justification at all for the statement he has made.

The right hon. gentleman must peruse the whole record and see all the letters that were written about that date, and it is quite clear that the amount referable about that time was $1.50. At first blush I thought it was $2.50, but on looking more closely I find it is $1.50. However, perhaps the Prime Minister can state what the value was that he placed upon it, which Mr. Fitzpatrick attributes to the right hon. gentleman. I did not attribute it to him, I only attribute it to him through Mr. Fitzpatrick, as appears from the correspondence.

In so far as I am concerned, I cannot say, at the present moment, what was the tenor of the conversation that I had with Mr. Fitzpatrick, or whether we discussed the value of the land-and of course we did as appears from his letter-or whether I thought it worth $1.50, or $1, or 80 cents. So far as I may have expressed any opinion upon the matter, it could not be my own individual opinion, because I do not pretend to know what the value of the land is, and I would not give my opinion as a land expert. I do not think I ever saw the land in question. I know, perhaps, the locality in which it is,

but I could not describe absolutely the locality in which it is situated. If the Solicitor General has made use of my opinion in this matter, I would expect the Solicitor General himself to declare what we discussed, because I have no recollection of what we did discuss.

Surely the right hon. Prime Minister cannot find any fault with me. I have simply taken the correspondence. If Mr. Fitzpatrick has made an unwarranted use of the Prime Minister's name, the fault lies with him and not with myself. As the correspondence will show, the price that Mr. Fitzpatrick was speaking of was $1.50 per square foot. The file goes ou to show that the cheques had been sent with the knowledge of Mr. Fitzpatrick to Quebec, and that then Mr. Couture had secured the services of Mr. Pugsley as solicitor. After dispensing with the services of Mr. Prefontaine, the price was increased from $1.50 to $2.50 a foot, and that is the contention that was made in the court.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word or two. I dislike very much to obtrude personal matters upon the House, but the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has on two occasions to-day charged me with impropriety in connection with the part I have taken in reference to one of the items under discussion this afternoon. I understand the hon. member to lay it down as a principle that no member of parliament should be concerned as solicitor or counsel in any claim against the Crown. If it is improper to do that, then I am in the company of very distinguished members of the profession who, for many years, sat on the same side of the House as that on which the hon. gentleman sits. I could name half a dozen members of the bar in Ontario and Quebec who were at the very top of their profession, where the hon. gentleman will take a very long time to get, and who did not consider it inconsistent with the dignity of the profession, or with the honour of parliament, to appear in a case in the Exchequer Court or the Supreme Court, or in a claim against a department. There is this further to be 'said in the matter of the Gilbert case, which the hon. gentleman took as an occasion for reading a lecture to myself, that it stands on a very different footing from other cases. If the hon. gentleman had taken the trouble to look into the position of this case, he would have seen that this claim arose out of a contract with the Department of Railways and Canals. One of the clauses of this contract provides that the chief engineer and deputy minister of the department shall be the sole judge to settle all claims arising under that contract. The chief engineer is constituted a judicial officer for the purpose of deciding all claims, such as the Gilbert claim, and his decision in the matter is final and conclusive, and when this matter was brought 178
up in the department in 1893, when I had not the honour of a seat in this House, * the matter was referred to the chief engineer, who is the present engineer, for investigation and report. At that time the political friends of the hon. gentleman were in power, and the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) was the Minister of Railways and Canals. My clients, for whom I had done business for many years, intimated to me that I was non persona grata to the then hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, and that it would be well to have some one else act in the matter who was more acceptable to the powers that were, and Mr. Ferguson, a prominent lawyer of Ottawa, for whom I entertained great respect, a strong political friend of the then hon. Minister of Railways and Canals was handed over my brief, and the work which I had done for many years for my clients. He prosecuted the claim for these people and secured a settlement of 15 per cent. It was an outrage if the hon. member for East Simcoe is right in his present view. But, when there was a change of government, and when I was no longer non persona grata, I think it was quite consistent with my duties, having acted for these people for years and years, not to go before the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and urge this claim as stated by the member for east Simcoe, but to go before his deputy, the chief engineer of the department, the poli-_ tical officer, sitting as a judge just as much as any judge in any of the courts in Canada, and to press for a decision by this officer in the manner and as provided in the said contract.
Hear, hear.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) laughs. What does he laugh at ?
I am laughing at the gratuitous insult you are tendering to the minister, that he is not in charge of his own department, but that the deputy runs it.

The hon. gentleman is too smart. If he knew anything about the contracts that are made with the Department of Railways and Canals, he would know that it is not the minister who has charge of the investigation of these claims, but he would know that contractors making contracts with that department agree that the chief engineer shall be the sole and only judge as to all claims arising out of their contracts. It was not the minister, but it was the deputy minister of the department, the chief engineer, who gave his certificate. It was upon his certificate that the minister came to the House and included this item in the estimates. The minister has no more to do with the matter than any other minister of the Crown who pronounced upon it in council, and he had no more to do with it in so far as this House is concerned



than the hon. gentleman has who stands up in this House and discusses it. The chief engineer was the sole and only judge. It was upon his certificate that it was decided to pay the amount, and the House subsequently voted the money with which to pay it. 1 would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he would apply the same rule he tried to have applied to me, to every member of this House ? If he does he will have to strike at an hon. member considerably higher than himself, because one of the very items was voted on this afternoon- I mean the claim of S. O'Donohue for $0,-222.27-was a claim in which his leader (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has been acting as counsel for the parties. I have the highest possible respect for the hon. leader of the opposition, and I know there is no man in this House, or In the profession, who entertains a higher opinion as to what is consistent with the dignity of the profession and the honour of parliament than that hon. gentleman does. Would the hon. member for East Simcoe assume to say that his leader was guilty of indecency and impropriety in allowing a claim of that kind to be pressed by the firm to which he belongs ? I would like to have an answer upon that.
When you are through.

My hon. friend acquiesces then ?
' Mr. BENNETT. No.

I think the attack made upon me was a most unfair and unjust one. After explaining to the satisfaction of the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) that this was an honest claim, after the ground was taken from under the feet of that hon. gentleman, the hon. member for East Simcoe gets up and attempts to lecture me in this House as to what is proper and dignified. I will tell him what I am prepared to do. This matter of members of the bar acting as counsel or as solicitors in one way or the other comes up for discussion occasionally. I will invite the members of the House who are members of the legal profession to a conference to decide once for all, and to arrive at an understanding, as to what is proper for a member of the bar to do before this House, or before committees of the House, or in the departments or in the courts of the country, and I warrant him that I shall be prepared to submit to the decision.
There are a large number of members in this House who belong to the legal profession, as do the hon. member for Simcoe and myself; men for whom I have the greatest respect, and if in their judgment it is inconsistent for a member of the legal profession who is a member of parliament, to act for clients to press their claims in the departments, or the Exchequer Court, or the Supreme Court, or any other court, where the government of Canada is con-Mr. BELCOURT.
cerned, I for one am prepared to submit to their judgment. But until such gentlemen, as the hon. leader of the opposition and other members who are lawyers of eminence in this House, say that I have been guilty of impropriety I am prepared to continue to do as I have done, notwithstanding the opinion of the member for East Simcoe.

Let me say that I have nothing to retract of what I have said this afternoon. It was not in personal animosity to the member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) that I mentioned his name. He was simply the accident of the conditions that exist, as was the member for Maisonueuve (Mr. Prefontaine) in his case. I have the honour to occupy a seat in this House for twelve sessions, and for the first time I have heard a member of parliament stand up and openly declare that he as a matter of right, should go before a department of government and before a minister and press a claim as solicitor.
Certainly.

The hon. member says ' certainly.' Now, I do not east any reflection upon the hon. gentleman's legal ability, nor do I say that he "would not have had this client even if he had not been a member; but I say that there is a strong leverage on those who have claims against the government to employ members of parliament who are in touch with the administration, be it Conservative or Liberal. That is where I say the thing is wrong. The hon. gentleman says that I find fault with him for prosecuting cases in courts against the Crown. Not at all. I find no such fault. There is nothing wrong in his appearing before judges where his political position can have no influence. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Belcourt) is not so young in politics as not to know of the insults that were heaped by the Liberal opposition on a leader of the Conservative party in Ontario, because he was retained on behalf of the government in a case.
The hon. gentleman knows that is prohibited by statute.

Whether it is or not,
I am speaking of the moral impropriety of such thing happening as I have described. In the case mentioned, the legal gentleman simply appeared before the courts, but here is a case where a member of parliament who is known to be in political touch with the party in power, goes before a minister and before a department to further a claim. The principle of that is wrong. It is unsound. It will not stand the broad glare of public opinion. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Belcourt) flung the gratuitous insult at me, that I have not a high political standing. So far as that is concerned I am quite satisfied with the political standing I have, and my financial necessities have never been such as to cause me to be a suppliant
]\IAY 20, 1901
or to have my name dangled before any government for any gift to be offered to a party friend. Perhaps the hon. gentleman for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) cannot say so much.
It will be a long time before anything of that kind is dangled before the hon. member (Mr. Bennett).
When the hon. member for Ottawa states that this case was argued before the chief engineer he makes a misstatement.
I am speaking of the present administration.

So am I. The hon. member (Mr. Belcourt) forgets the debates last session and the production of the quasi report of the chief engineer in support of his claim. He forgets that Mr. Rubidge the engineer in charge of this particular work was called to the department, and in consultation with the minister made a report to which the chief engineer gave a quasi endorsation. The case must have been argued before the minister and the engineer in charge of this work, particularly if it was argued before the persons who formed the judgment upon it. We all know that the law requires the chief engineer to certify to the validity of such a claim.
I don't think the member for East Simcoe knows that much.

The hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) misstated the facts as regards the argument. The chief engineer defended himself by accepting the report of Mr. Rubidge, and the report shows that it was in consultation between Mr Rubidge and the minister that the report was formed.

This discussion has disclosed a state of affairs that is a scandal m this House and in this country. Prom day to day we have disclosures as to the course taken by members on the government benches in regard to public business. Here the member for Ottawa, unable to deny, turns around and glories in the fact that he is using his services as member of parliament to promote the interests of contractors, and those who have business arrangements with the government. It is a scandal and a disgrace which should be put an end to at once. This member for Ottawa (Mr Belcourt) says, that if he has erred, he has erred in good company, and that he has yet to discover that it is wrong for a member of parliament to appear against the Crown. My friend from East Simcoe has pointed out that a lawyer has a right to go with his clients to the Exchequer Court or the Supreme Court or any court in the empire, but he has no right to go lobbving around the departments to try to get "business through in that way, or to go to the Auditor 178*
General to attempt to bulldoze him. It is degrading for a member of this House. It is illegal. We saw this same member of parliament the other day the open advocate of the Bell Telephone Company in this House. Did he get a fee for tliat ? Is he the solicitor of the Bell Telephone Company ?
It is none of your business.

Ah. It is none of our business. So long as a member conducts his affairs outside of this House it is none of our business, but when he comes to the floor of this House of Commons and advocates such claims it becomes our business. Yes, Sir, there is the open confession again. There is a hon. member who cannot deny that he was the advocate of the Bell Telephone Company. And what was the Bell Telephone Company coming to parliament for ? They were applying for a series of flagrant demands that would be injurious to the whole people of this Dominion. Yet, Sir, we find their advocate in the House of Commons; their solicitor, presumedly with a fee in his pocket to advocate their interests. Sir, men of that kind should be driven out of the House of Commons instead of being allowed to pursue their mercenary objects in this Chamber.

I am very sorry to see that this serious state of affairs is taken with so much levity, as if a member of this House could take a fee to advocate anything before the Minister of Railways and Canals or before his deputy, and not be ashamed of it. There is no possible objection to any lawyer appearing before the Supreme Court or before any of the judges ; but I say that a member of this House, be he a member of the legal or any other profession, has no right to take a fee for appearing before any committee of this House or before any deputy of a department. I think it is a very serious state of affairs indeed, and is not 1o be laughed at or taken lightly. There are perh-aps twenty or thirty lawyers on the gov-emment side of this House, and perhaps an equal number on this side ; and if it is to be assumed that one of these gentlemen may take a fee and advocate his client's interest here, subordinating his position as a member of this House to the interest of his client, a very small amount of money would carry a vote of this House for any measure. I do not think it is possible that this matter can be too seriously considered and discussed. It has probably been done thoughtlessly ; but I say it is a serious matter if any legal member of this House, especially a member on the government side, can take a fee from any company or individual to advocate a claim before any department of the government. I do not say that that has been done ; but the tendency of the discussion to-night indicates that that state of affairs does not appear to be seriously thought of
*

by many members, as I think it ought to be.
I should be sorry indeed to suppose that members of the legal profession should think so lightly of their position as members of the parliament of Canada as to take a fee to advocate any measure before any bead of a department.
Might I ask the hon. member who has just taken his seat if he is not a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company ?

Yes, I am a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and I will defy any member of this House to show any occasion on which I have, by word, by deed, by canvassing or by vote, in any shape or way, advocated any measure in which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has been interested from the day I came to this House down to this day.

If the hon. gentleman is sincere in the lecture he has attempted to give to the legal members of this House, then he ought to resign either as a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or as a member of this House. I do not mind being lectured by such a high-minded, honourable, fair-minded and unprejudiced man as the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace). Such an unprejudiced, fair-minded gentleman has a right to lecture anybody in this House. But when it comes down to being lectured by a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, who is also a member of this House, there I draw the line.

I am sorry that the opinion I have expressed as to the light manner in which this idea is held by the legal fraternity, as represented by the last speaker, is true. He apparently does not see that there is any evil in it. He has made the charge against me that I am a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I am, and, I am proud of it. At the same time, if my interest as a Canadian Pacific Railway director at any time conflicts with my duty to the country, I will resign one or other of these positions.
You ought to resign now.
I repeat that my interest as a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway has never conflicted with my duty to the country.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen may laugh just as they like ; but I say that I have never by word or by deed advocated any interest of the Canadian Pacific Railway in this House. I have never voted on any Bill in which the Canadian Pacific Railway has been interested, and I have never canvassed nor spoken to any member of this House on behalf of anything connected with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; and I defy any member of this House to give
one single instance in which in any shape or way I have not fulfilled my duty as a member of this House.

I want to say just one word with reference to the statement made by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. It appears to me that only in the last session of this parliament I heard the hon. gentleman denounce the granting of railway subsidies to other railway companies, and that was done in the interest of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I have never heard him denounce any subsidy that was proposed to be granted to the Canadian Pacific Railway ; but when any subsidy was proposed to be granted to any other railway corporation in this country, the hon. gentleman denounced it in unmeasured terms, and held up his hands in holy horror at the idea of railway subsidies. The hon. gentleman has forgotten the amount of money the firm of Osier, Hammond and Nanton got out of the Calgary and Edmonton Railway or the Regina, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway. After all that money has gone into their coffers, it is easy for the hon. gentleman to get up and talk about other people advocating interests.
I think it is hardly worth while replying to the hon. gentleman ; but I wish to say for years before I came into this House I denounced railway subsidies.
Except for the Canadian Pacific Railway.

I denounced them for the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I think it was a great mistake for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to accept subsidies other than the subsidies they got for the main line. I have always been against granting railway subsidies and against railway *companies accepting subsidies. I have had no connection, directly or indirectly, with any company receiving railway subsidies since I became a member of this House.
Intercolonial Railway, $400,000.

This is an item towards operating expenses in addition to the main vote.
Public building, Dawson, $30,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How much has already been appropriated ?

I intend instructing the chief architect to go
\

to the other side and look at the plans for a mint, and also at buildings that are numerous on the other side, so as to devise the best plan for the Victoria Museum. From what I can see, the mint will cost in the neighbourhood of $300,000.
The Minister of Finance said $200,000.

I said the building would cost $200,000, and the Inclosure and strong rooms, machinery, &c., would bring it up to $300,000.
Parliament Buildings-Addition to building over engine-house, and improvements for main vestibule, including two electric elevators, $35,000.

Ever since I entered parliament I have heard complaints, and legitimate complaints, that we Iliad no proper accommodation. I intend to carry out plans that have been submitted to me by the chief architect by erecting a building right over the engine-house. There will be seven rooms, three on the ground floor, three on the second floor and one at the top, the upper room having a floor area of 60 x 40 fefet. We shall also have two elevators, one from the Senate entrance and one from the House of Commons entrance opening upon the large lobby just where the post office is. The chief architect has asked to be allowed to carry out the work himself. He knows the building well and is conver-isant with the work to be carried out. I think this accommodation will be appreciated by hon. members on both sides. The new building will not interfere with the light or ventilation of the House, and some of the six rooms that will be available, I hope to offer to my hon. friends on the other side who have complained.

I was just going to object. The distribution of rooms has not been to any extent to the advantage of the opposition. We have no rooms except the leader's room, the whips' room and one other. I think it is not right to have such an unfair distribution. If the six rooms in this new building-the top one I suppose will be for committee purposes-are to be for the convenience of supporters of the government, I enter my strong protest against it as an unfair use of public money.
We have given to the opposition the very same accommodation that we have ourselves.
That is not true.

Why does the hon. member (Mr. Wallace) use that language here ? Of course, he is perfectly welcome to it, but he is wrong. I am right in what I say, with this single exception-that the room that was allowed to the Hon. Mr. Foster has been given to the
hon. member for Victoria, N.B. (Hon. Mr. Costigan). Except for that, hon. gentlemen opposite have the same accommodation that we have. But members have not proper accommodation-and that is the reason why we are most anxious to provide other rooms. But there is no use in using strong language.
I do not see why we should have any hard feeling here.

We object to the hon. member for Victoria, N.B. (Mr. Costigan), having room that was formerly occupied by Hon. Mr. Foster. I would like to know what rights the hon. member for Victoria, N.B., has in this House over any other government supporter from the province of New Brunswick ? Are rooms so plentiful that one gentleman should be given a room to himself ? If so, then, why are so many of us crowded into No. G ? In saying this, :I do not wish to uphold the way the late government treated their opponents for they were not generous enough in their treatment of them. But, the hon. gentlemen opposite, having had that experience years ago, ought to be generous enough, now, after one term in office, to give us a better distribution of the rooms at their disposal. And. while I am on my feet, I would like to draw attention to the fact that room No. G is a small room, and that the room adjoining it might be devoted to the use of those who occupy No. 6, an archway being cut between.
What room is that ?
The room the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte) occupies.
Oh, no ; I will keep that for myself.

Why could the hon. gentleman' not take a room in the new building atijd thus leave his room free to be given over to the use of those who occupy No. 6 ? There is another point-the leader of the opposition and the Conservative whips occupy two rooms which are separated by only one" room from No. G. This intervening room is occupied by an officer of the House. Why not give him a room occupied by the whips and give his room to the whips ? This would suit the Conservative party in this House much better than the present arrangement.

When these additional seven rooms are built, I shall have much pleasure in conferring with the leaders of the opposition as to the distribution of them. We are here three or four months of the year and I believe it is our duty to be as comfortable as we cau.

I am sorry that the Minister of Public Works when he was about it did not decide upon a radical change. The rooms for the accommodation of members of parliament are entirely insufficient. We have none of accommodation,

none of the privileges, none of the luxuries, I may say, afforded to the members of nearly every other parliament in the world. We want a far larger building. I was in hopes that the minister would decide to add a wing to the back of this building which would not have interfered with the architectural beauty of the structure, and would have given greater accommodation to the Speaker, besides giving us space, for at least tea-room and for some of the accommodation of a club for hon. members. It is ridiculous, it is wrong, that nothing has been done in that direction. I admit that 'the government of which I was member were to blame for not taking action in the matter. But, with the buoyant revenue that the government now have, this change might be undertaken. I believe that it would be according to the wishes of nearly every member if additional room were provided so that we could have something in the form of a club-house, something after the style of what they have in the British House'of Commons-but not nearly so extravagant- something in the style of what they have at Washington or what they have in nearly every state capitol in the United States. It improves our morals, it has a tendency, anyway, to improve the morale of the whole House. I would like to strengthen the hands [DOT]of the Minister of Public Works on this opportunity. If he can persuade his colleagues to do something in that direction, I am sure it would meet the wishes of nearly the whole House.

I have felt for a long time, not only since I am a member of this parliament, but when I was a member of the press gallery, that the accommodation is altogether inadequate, that it is not even worthy of this nation. We have a great many foreign visitors,' and we often see people that we would like to entertain, but on account of lack of accommodation in these buildings we cannot do it. I have received a petition signed by influential members of parliament on both sides of the House, asking for more accommodation, and it will be my duty, or the duty of somebody else, to look into that question. I feel that it is a matter that must be taken up immediately. A great many things have been said' about the Jesuits, but they have one motto which is a thoroughly good one : mens sana in cor-pore sano, in other words, a sound mind in a sound body. To work well you must have the body well fed. and you must occupy pleasant premises. If I remain in the position I now occupy, I will make it my duty during the recess to look carefully into the improvements that the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals has suggested, and which I believe will meet the approbation of both sides of the House, of all those in fact who travel and realize that the world moves.
Mr. HAGGART

I was one of those who objected when our friends were in power because I thought that a proper proportion of the rooms was not given to the opposition. My opinion always has been that the opposition should have a share of the rooms according to their numbers. I hoped when the Liberal party came to power they would be more generous in that respect than their predecessors had been, because they had always preached fair-play in opposition. But I regret to say that instead of being fairer than the Conservatives were, it is just the reverse, for they have not given the present opposition the same proportion of rooms that the supporters of the present government had when they were in opposition.
You have the rooms I have mentioned.

We have no rooms at all except the one occupied by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals and one or two of ids friends. The wThip occupies one room, the leader of the opposition occupies one, and there is room No. 6 as the general assembly room of the party.
There is room 40 upstairs.

I say that outside of those I have mentioned, there is only one room that is accorded to the rank and file of the party. I regard the treatment of the opposition in this respect as a great injustice to the private members on our side of the House. Private members have no place in these premises where they can work. True, they can go down to their rooms in the hotels, but that necessitates a constant messenger service between them and the House. I really expected more generosity from the Minister of Public Works than has been accorded to us. With regard to the room he proposes to make, I understand him to say that it will not interfere with the light or ventilation of this House. I cannot understand how that is possible, because if he is filling up the whole of that space
Only a part of it. It does not interfere with a single window of the House.
Can the minister tell us what will be the size of the new premises ?
The width will be 26 feet and the length 60. It does not interfere with the light, I have inspected the locality myself.
I cannot see how we can hdve a building 20 by 60 without affecting the light.

It will not affect the ventilation or the light at all. If my hon. friend will go into the

lobby he can see for himself that it will not interfere with a single window. I have inspected the situation myself with the chief architect and the Minister of Finance.
If you put up a building you must necessarily obstruct the passage of the air, at least in some measure.

Without measuring, I think the minister proposes to fill up about one-third of the space. It will not affect the light. At first I thought it would, and I had the matter explained to me by the minister, and I became satisfied that it will not affect the light. As to ventilation^ suppose that you fill up even one-third of the space, there will possibly be less air moving, but still you do not obstruct the windows from which you got both light and ventilation.
The chief architect, who is an able man, can be trusted as to that.

I understand from the Minister of Public Works that he is about to rearrange this building in order to give increased accommodation to those gentlemen who are applying for it. I think it is pretty late in the day for these gentlemen to apply for room. The minister will remember that I made application for a room for the Independent party almost the first day I came to this House, and the Minister of Public Works has not yet told me that he would give me a room. I want to know from him now whether he intends to provide the Independent party with a room or not, because I think the Independent party in this House is just as important as any other party in it. I think, perhaps, the Independent party has contributed as much to the benefit of this country as any party, and I think we ought to be recognized. If we are not recognized it is quite possible you may hear from us. After the next election it is quite possible there may be a very much larger number of Independents here and it is also possible that an effort may be made to get their assistance. It is likely, after what transpired in this House to-day, that there will be a very much larger number of Independents in this House. There is a large number now, but many of them have hesitated to declare themselves to me. Many of them have said: Mr. Robinson, I am with you; but they are hidebound and they say :	I pi'omised my
party that I would vote for that party, but I am with you in many of the things that you have introduced into this House. We expect that the hon. Minister of Public Works will get a room for the Independents.
He says he is going to put you in the tower.

He will never put me in the tower, because he knows I do not misbehave myself like some of these
hen. gentlemen around here. I can do all my writing in my seat as I have done it, but sometimes I want to think and when I do I would like to do it alone. Therefore, I think I am entitled and that the Independent party are entitled to a room as much as other hon. gentlemen who have made such a pathetic appeal.

It will be my pleasure to supply a room to the Independent members during the next session. My hon. friend (Mr. Robinson, Elgin), I have no doubt, will prove, as he has already begun to prove, that he is quite capable to be the leader of the Independent party. We cannot have any more genuine leader of an Independent party than he is and I would say again that it will be my pleasure to supply our Independent friends with a room commensurate with their usefulness.
When will this building be ready ?

About the 1st of January or December.
Mr. 'WALLACE. Of this year ?
Yes, before the next meeting of parliament.

If it were a little later, still it would not make much difference because we will probably be on the other side of the House and be able to adjust these rooms more fairly than they are apportioned at the present time. I would make another suggestion to the hon. minister. Look here, Mr. Chairman, when a member is addressing the committee you should recognize his rights.
