speechtext: The clerk simply asked me what item we were at and I said we were now considering No. 53, and that the next would be No. 54. That is exactly what passed.

That is not what occurred before that. However, I was addressing the Chair and I was going on to suggest to the minister what appears to me to be a better solution of the difficulty of providing more room, if more room is required and more room is required. Walking up towards

the front building it has always strade me that this building was too low, too squatlooking in appearance and that it might be raised one storey with advantage to its architectural appearance, and to the convenience of the members ot the House of Commons and the officers who must necessarily be in this building. X presume the architects and officers of the hon. gentleman's department have considered this matter and that he may have considered it himself. It occurred to me that when putting these elevators in you could make that third storey immediately and conveniently available and that the architectural appearance of the building would be very greatly enhanced.

When the west block was destroyed three years ago I had a plan made with another storey added and having consulted with the engineer and a good many friends, my colleagues and others, we came to the conclusion that the addition of a storey would spoil the whole thing.
I think so in regard to the west block but that is not m regard to this building.

Well, I do not believe there is any architect who would venture to adopt the plan that the hon. gentleman is suggesting now. The architecture of this building is so relined that I would not venture to touch it in anyway. I do not believe that the plan would be 'adopted at all. The only thing is to have a new building, and the idea that has been suggested by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals will be carefully studied during the recess. It would give additional accommodation. I think the proposed plan will be sufficient for years to come. We all recognize that another public building should be erected as soon as possible. We have so much money to spend on public buildings here in Ottawa that it is difficult for the Minister of Public Works to ask for more, it would have been difficult this year to have asked for more than has been asked foir. I have the mint and the Victoria Museum buildings and these will cost a large amount of money. Next year if the revenue is buoyant, as I hope it will be, we may perhaps think of another building which would enable us to get rid of these buildings that we rent.

Mr. Chairman, while the matter of changes and the study of proposed changes in connection with this building is likely to engage the attention^ of the hon. Minister of Public Works during the recess, as I understand it is, would it not be of tbe highest importance to the members of this House that some careful study of the ventilation of this Chamber should be made by the department ? The standard of health of the members of tills House is really, I think, low. There is a

large percentage of members who are more or less ill every session. I am sure this is very largely owing to the fact that this Chamber is not ventilated at all. 1 occasionally go into tlie gallery of the House during the afternoon session and if the House is at all crowded and the galleries are crowded it requires no other evidence than one's nose to tell him that the Chamber is absolutely without ventilation. This is not, to my mind, altogether creditable to the government management in the fact that _ they have consigned some 200 members of parliament, who are selected, I presume, for their mental capacity and placed them in what is practically a pit, in a low Chamber, surrounded by high walls without ventilation. The effect of the atmosphere, which we have to breathe and in which we have to live and work during the months of the session, is paralyzing 1 It is destructive to the health of members and it prevents them from making the highest possible use of their faculties. It causes, to my mind, a very large amount of illness, because 1 am sure every hon. member of the House must have observed that there is an unusually large percentage of members who are ill during the session. It strikes me that tbe most important thing to consider is not the finding of rooms for the convenience of members, or tbe finding of tea rooms to enable them to cultivate the amenities of social life, but to give them wholesome atmosphere in which they may work and breathe.
To my mind, the atmosphere of the House of Commons, when the Chamber and the galleries are at all crowded, is almost poisonous. The Minister of Public W orks should employ some sanitary expert to make a careful study of the conditions of ventilation in this building, and during tbe session samples of tbe air should be collected from different parts of the Chamber and analysed. If that were done it would demonstrate at once that we are living in a poisonous atmosphere. It is exceedingly injurious. It prevents the highest ability of the members being developed, and it is a bar on the activity of parliament. We are living right on the bank of tlie river, with its currents of pure air in abundance, and some rational system should be adopted by which the foul air would be drawn out of this Chamber and the fresh air admitted. Every medical man will agree with me that it is a reform which should receive the attention of the government at once, and that it should not be spoken of in this Chamber, and then dismissed from the thoughts of tbe responsible ministers.

We have no fresh air from the outside except we open these windows, and then my hon. friends opposite say I want to kill them all with the draught. That is not my intention at all ; it is very far from it, indeed ; I want to see them live long.
The minister does not say that the ventilation of this Chamber is an impossibility ?
1 am not an expert.
Then, I am not unreasonable in asking the minister to employ an expert ?
The chief architect, who is a man of very long experience, tells me that every possible device has been tried.

If any man in a good condition of health comes out of the open air and goes into that gallery at any time the House is in session, his nose will tell him that he is living in an atmosphere saturated with organic matter that is unfit to breath. There is no other reform of such importance in connection with these buildings as the supplying of fresh air to the Commons of Canada.
To authorize commencement of the construction of the Victoria Memorial Museum, $50,000.
What is expected to be the whole cost of that museum ? Is the minister asking for competitive plans for the construction of that building :

I have here the plans which have been prepared by the chief architect. If we erect only a museum, the chief architect believes it will cost about $500,000 ; but, if with the museum we include a Supreme Court, Exchequer Court, National Art Gallery and Fishery Exhibit, it will cost more. I beg to invite hon. gentlemen to look at these plans.
Where is the building to be erected ?

In Major's Hill park, opposite the corner of Mackenzie avenue and St. Patrick street. We will not be obliged to buy land. That is only a suggestion, of course. I have made up my mind to send the chief architect to Europe to look at plans. Although he has been there already, I think he should go to the other side to see the museums in Paris, London, Dublin, Vienna and elsewhere. I have seen some very fine museums there. You cannot buy property in Ottawa unless you pay a high price indeed. You would be obliged to pay $80,000, or perhaps $100,000, for a site. If the museum would be built in Major's Hill park it would be a fine situation.

Would it be considered any reflection on the architect of the department if the minister were to ask for competitive plans for this building ? If it is intended to expend half a million dollars, I think that would be a good policy, with respect to the whole group of buildings.

I would not consider it at all a reflection
on my architect to ask for competitive plans. That is a fair suggestion.

It seems to me that some settled plan ought to be submitted to the House, and some information with regard to the location of the museum before we vote very much money for it. Otherwise we may find after the work has been commenced that it should be located somewhere else or that some different plan should have been adopted. I think it would be well to advance slowly with an undertaking of such gigantic magnitude.

I do not at all object to having competitive plans. We have had competition for the statue of Her Majesty. But I think the House will agree with me that it will be wise to instruct the chief architect to visit some of the best museums on the other side of the ocean, and then I shall be quite prepared to ask for competitive plans. 1 believe I can be trusted to do the right thing on these lines. I do not profess myself to be an expert, although I have visited a good many museums in my life.

I understand from the minister that the intention is to have plans drawn for a building which will be like that shown in the plan on the Table, comprising a museum, rooms for the Supreme Court, the fisheries exhibit, and so on-a general art building. If this is the intention, I for one am thoroughly in accord with it, and 1 hope it will be taken up with the purpose of having eventually, when it is finished, a building which will be not only suitable for all these objects, but creditable to the country. I do not think the country will grudge a proper expenditure in order to give us a creditable building.

I may say that I have no fixed plan. The plan before the House is only a tentative one. Whether we should have a museum by itself or couple some other departments with it is an open question. We shall have to provide further accommodation in the way of public buildings. A suitable site for another public building would be that where the Supreme Court now stands. We could have a fine public building located there. I have gone into that question with the chief architect. I have no hesitation in saying that the idea of competitive plans is most acceptable to me.
Is it the intention to expend any part of the money you are now taking before you decide what buildings you will erect ?
No, I will not spend a dollar before we make up our minds altogether.

I confess I am not at all favourably impressed with the site the minister has chosen. It appears to me

tliat it would be a great pity to hide such a beautiful building as has been represented to us in such au out-of-tlie-way place. 1 think the minister should endeavour to find a location commensurate with the character and appearance of the building. Surely he can find a location somewhere on the government grounds; or, if not, I would certainly say, let us pay a reasonable sum of money for a site on which the building will show to decidedly better advantage than would be the case on a back street in Lower Town.

I cannot share the view of my bon. friend.
I believe the site I have suggested is a very acceptable one. If my hon. friend, in taking his early promenade to-morrow morning, will go in that direction, he will find that the site is a very fine one indeed. Major Hill Park is a fine park; we are going to improve it year by year; it is near at hand and approachable; and the intention later on is to erect a bridge across the ravine to connect it with the grounds here.
I think there could not be a more suitable site found about the place. It is roomy and picturesque. All that is required is a bridge.

I understand that the site was opposite the Printing Bureau, on the lower part of Major Hill Park. Would it not be possible to have the building erected on this side of the park so as to be visible and accessible from these grounds ?

I quite agree with the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson). If you are going to have the building on the low land in front of the Printing Bureau, you will hide the beauty of the building and will have it in an inconvenient and to some extent inaccessible place, whereas, if it is put on the high ground, and there seems to be ample room for it, it will be a very desirable ornament to Major Hill Park.

As I have been for many years a resident of Ottawa, I would venture to make a suggestion in the hope that the hon. minister will consider it before finally deciding on the location. In my opinion, the best place for the museum would be on Nepean Point, immediately behind where the cannons are placed to-day. You have there a very high ground which naturally forms part of the Major Hill Park. It is not to-day included in the park, but I think it ought to be. It is government property, and in choosing that site the govern- i ment would have nothing to pay for the ' lot. A building erected on that point would ' command a view far and wide on all sides, 1 and be perceived at a very great distance 1 from the city, at every approach to it. I 1 have given the matter some consideration : and gone over the ground, and I offer this 1 Mr. HENDERSON.
1 suggestion, in the hope that the minister i will consider it before coming to a final dei cision.
J Mr. EDWARDS. I think that Major Hill j Park and Nepean Point ought to be abso-I lately reserved for park purposes. It was a . mistake to have erected the Printing Bureau f at Nepean Point. My opinion is that the 1 museum should be erected at some point j distant from the parliament buildings-in the southern portion of the city, for instance. A good piece of ground could be got there, and it would be a much more suitable lo-
[DOT]	cality for this edifice.

Is it intended that the , selection of the site will be made before
[DOT] next session and the building begun ?
1 The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
I think that the site will be chosen and the
*	building begun before the session. But I : do not intend to rely on my own little 1 knowledge for the selection of the site and ' the plans. I know that my architect is an
able man, and is not afraid to consult archi-: tects and other men of experience. As this . building will be a national affair, I am determined not to do anything before my colleagues and myself are convinced that we have made the best selection of site and
*	plans.

Before expending so much money, this House should be given the opportunity of passing upon the plans. The hon. gentleman tells us that we may have three buildings in one, or only one building. It may be a building for the museum alone, or it may comprise the Supreme Court and Exchequer Court, and some other buildings. We are committing ourselves to an expenditure without having any idea what will be the full amount we may be called on to spend. I do not think it would be proper to commit the country to this expenditure until this House has had the opportunity of passing upon the plans and coming to a conclusion whether they will have the three buildings in one or make but one building.

Parliamentary government implies a certain number of gentlemen who, for the time being, enjoy the confidence of the majority of the House. This is the essence of parliamentary government, and I am very much afraid my hon. friend will have to trust the present government. He may rest assured that we will not enter into a useless expenditure of money.

I differ from the hon. gentleman in his view of parliamentary government. I have always understood that when the government propose an expenditure of public money, they are bound to submit to the House the information which would enable it to deal intelligently with the question before authorizing the expenditure. The erection of this building will cost about half

a million dollars, and I would not regard it as the highest act of parliamentary government for any minister to enter into that contract and commit this House to it without first having the sanction of parliament.
If we erect only a museum we will not spend more than $500,000. I will send the chief architect to the other side to look at the best museums in the world.

Has the Iron, gentleman and his colleagues settled yet what kind of building they propose to erect ? There is no urgent necessity for going on with this in the next few months, and in the meantime it would be w'-ell to have the plans submitted and executed for submission before beginning the undertaking.

I differ with my hon. friend altogether. There is great urgency. In fact, we have been criminal in delaying the erection of this building so long. We have the finest collection of minerals on the continent exposed every day to be destroyed.

The hon. minister ought to have a definite plan and submit that plan to the House before he goes on with the work. We ought to know whether this *building is to be for the museum alone or for the museum and the Supreme and Exchequer Courts and the fishery building. We have a Supreme and an Exchequer Court now, which practically fill all the requirements, and also a fishery building, which is conveniently located and answers the purpose very well. I do not see what we want of a new Supreme Court, or Exchequer Court, or fishery building. The minister is not prepared to tell the House whether he is going on with them or not. We should not be asked to g-o it blind, but the minister should come here with a definite statement.

In matters of this kind in which we are not expert, I do not like to be too positive. As I have decided to send the chief architect to the other side, I thought the House would trust me by allowing me some latitude.
But, the hon. gentleman is sending the chief architect to the other side to see about a museum, and not about a Supreme Court or a fishery building.

But, if the chief architect found that, with an addition of, say, $200,000, he could provide for these branches of the public ser-vict also, I should like the House to trust me in that matter. At the same time, my impression is that we shall erect only a museum.

I think the House would trust the hon. gentleman so far as his personal integrity goes, or even his judgment.
But, what I am contending for is a principle of government. In a great undertaking involving the expenditure of a million dollars, the work should not be gone on with before parliament has passed judgment upon it, after definite plans and full information submitted to the House.

I am much surprised at file objection raised by the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace). If there is one thing above ail others that might be said to be a disgrace to this country, it is the fact that the highest court in the Dominion is housed in the old stables that they have occupied for a number of years. The buildings are not only unsuitable in ,eyery other way, but they are unsanitary. I think the Minister of Public Works is to be highly commended for the efforts he is putting forth to have new rooms for the Supreme Court of Canada. As to the fishery building, it is located in a part of the city that is within the lire zone, as we may call it. very near the centre of the city. The building is not suitable, it is not of sufficient capacity-
It is ugly.

It certainly is. And it will grow more unsuitable, for we hope that this exhibit will be added to from year to year. Then, as to the museum, we all know that the other night, if the wind had been in a different quarter, the chances are that the Dominion of Canada would have been without the contents of a museum. The point suggested by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr, Belcourt) appeals to me very strongly. If this building is to be erected, regard must be had to the public advantage. Such a public building should be as isolated as possible consistent with public convenience, and I do not know any spot that would be more suitable and more compatible with the requirements and surroundings than Nepean Point. I agree with the hon. member for Ottawa, that it would be a pity to destroy the park by having this building, or any other building, no matter how artistic, erected in it. I believe xue suggestion of the Minister of Public Works should receive the unanimous support of the House. I trust that the buildings as planed will be erected, and that not a moment will be lost in carrying out the work.
Rainy River-Lock and dam (revote), $25,000.
Has anything been done there ?

No, nothing has been done. I intend toj make a personal inspection of the river, and I will not start the work until I am sure it can be carried out successfully. Before starting, we must arrange with the American authorities, as the river is the boundary line between the United States and us.
*56S7
This work is rendered necessary by the fact that Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann are going to have their terminals there. We are enlarging our breakwater to give them more accommodation.
Will that be done by contract ?
Yes.
Will this amount finish the work ?

I think it will about finish it, but I am not sure.
Telegraph Lines-British Columbia-Land line, Port Simpson via Port Essington to Hazleton, $40,000.

I have a map here which will show the location of these lines, and which I offer to the inspection of my friends. From Port Simpson to Hazelton is 180 miles. Of that distance 150 miles are already built. I received a telegram from Mr. Charleson a day or two ago to the effect that 150 miles are built. Port Essington and Port Simpson are both on Canadian territory. When these lines are built, we will have 2.000 miles of telegraph lines on Canadian soil.
Branch line from a point on the Quesnelle-Atlin line about fifteen miles east of Port Fraser to Manson Creek, $48,000.
Is Mr. Charleson building that line also ?

Yes, the wire is there, and some other supplies have been bought. The whole thing will ue completed by the loth of July this year.
Public Buildings-Nova Scotia-Arichat-Reconstruction of public building, $3,000.

There has been a public building at Arichat for some years, a wooden building, which is in a state of decay, and which it is proposed to reconstruct. It will be used as a post office and customs-ihouse.
Halifax-Drill hall, $6,900.
The plans are ready, and we are going to ask for tenders.
What do you expect this building will cost ?

About $200,000 inclusive of the site. It is for post office, custom-house and excise building. The site will cost $25,000. The site will be 86 by 107 by 103 feet, and will form three sides of a quadrangle.
Mr. TARTE
Public Buildings-New Brunswick-Marysville -Public building (revote), $8,000.
Do all these public buildings contain post office and customhouse ?

Yes, all of them, and in addition, some of them will supply room for an armoury.
Richibucto-Public building, $4,000.
What is the population of Richibucto ?
About 3,000, I think.
Is that the total expenditure intended for a public building ?

Yes. Some time ago the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) and some other members suggested that it would be a good idea to erect a larger number of public buildings and less costly, and I am just beginning to try my hand at it. My hon. friend will find in these estimates several amounts for cheap public buildings, but a large number of them.
Quebec-Immigrant buildings on Louise embankment and Queen's wharf buildings, $4,500.
Is that for repairs ?
There is one of these buildings on Queen's wharf that was destroyed by fire. We are taking a very small amount for repairs. The balance is for rebuilding the structure which was destroyed.
Are you letting the work by contract ?

Yes, the work is now being done. The amount of the contract is $2,300.
Quebec-Post Office-Renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $3,000.
What renewals ?

All sorts of renewals, floors, painting, &c. Repairs might be a better word.
Montreal-Post Office-Improvements, $1,500.

I would like to ask the lion. Minister of Public Works, in connection with this item and the following one whicli have appeared almost every year for alterations and repairs to the Montreal public buildings since I have sat in this House, and which involves an expenditure of from $10,000 to $15,000 a year, has it not occurred to him that it would be better for the government to acquire a building in Montreal V We are paying out a considerable amount for rent there and we are expending a good deal every year for repairs. I remember that three or four years ago I suggested ' to the hon. Minister of Public Works the advisability and necessity, instead of spend-

ing that large sum every year on repairs in addition to the rent we are paying in Montreal, that we should acquire a building there for the use of the government. I believe the government is very much cramped for space in Montreal. There is a considerable amount spent for renewals. Has the point never been examined by the hon. gentleman as to whether it would not be cheaper to own a building ?

I quite grant that we are cramped for room, that the post office building does not afford the accommodation that a large city like Montreal expects, but at the same time,
I have always hesitated about trying to buy other property. I fully admit that the hon. gentleman's suggestion is worthy of consideration. We do not pay high rentals in Montreal. Of course, the post office, the examining warehouse, and the custom house are our own property. We pay rent only for the branches, and we do not pay any other rentals. I quite recognize that we will have in the near future to acquire more space; in point of fact, at the present time the postal authorities have asked me if we could not find accommodation in the Canadian Pacific Railway station for the delivery of letters and newspapers. As soon as the session is over I will look carefully into that. The hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock) has made in Toronto an arrangement that is working very well indeed, and perhaps we will be able to make the same arrangement in Montreal. I quite admit that we must do something in the near future in Montreal. We know that the post office does not afford the accommodation we require there.
The Department of Railways and Canals pays a good deal for rent there. It is obliged to rent a whole flat ?

Yes.
Grosse Isle-Quarantine station, $20,000.
What is this for ?

We are putting in at the quarantine station a waterworks system which is very badly needed. They are obliged to take the water from the St. Lawrence and it is salt water, and we require to have a condenser. We are completing this waterworks system now. I am sorry that we have not completed it sooner, because at the present time there is a large number of people located there.
This is to complete ?

Yes, and to make it, I believe, the best sanitary station on this continent.
Montreal - Public Buildings - Improvements, alterations, repairs, &c., $10,000.
This is the item I referred to a moment ago as occurring every year.

I have the details of the work. Every year the chief architect receives from the different branches that are located in Montreal demands for improvements and changes and we are only carrying out the demands made upon us.
St, Hyacinthe-Drill hall, $10,000.
This is a new work.
Has the site been decided upon for the St. Hyacinthe drill hall ?
No, I intend to' go there myself and consult with my colleague from the Militia and Defence Department.
It would be well to consult with somebody else there too, because, as the hon. minister is aware, there is a considerable controversy as to the site.

I intend also consulting with the citizens.
Levis-Public building, $10,000.
What is the public building for ?
It will be for the post office, custom office, excise office-a public building for general use.
What is the population ? The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. Between 10,000 and 12,000. It is a large town.
What is this building expected to cost ?

I do not expect to spend much money on this building, or on other public buildings for which I am asking votes from parliament this year. I may as well take advantage of the opportunity of making a statement on this subject. After _ consultation, we have come to the conclusion that perhaps we have spent too much money in the past on public buildings. Both political parties may have erected too c expensive buildings, and I shall try to erect less expensive ones. I believe I can get businesslike buildings erected for a moderate amount of money. The great trouble is that my hon. friend's on the other side of the House-I cannot blame them very much, because I was with them then-have erected buildings that have cost large amounts of money and -when I am asking my friends on this side of the House to practice economy they point to buildings here and there that have cost large amounts of money. All the same, I will resist the pressure and I will try to erect buildings that will not cost too much money. I will try to have an

economical and businesslike plan that will answer the public purposes without costing too much. At Levis I do not Intend to spend more than $12,000 or $15,000, and I believe that with that amount of money I can erect a very suitable building.
Montreal-Custom-house-Alterations, &c., $7,000.
We appear to spend about $35,000 for repairing public buildings in Montreal.
We have very large buildings there.
Will all these repairs be done by contract and tender ?

Oh, no. They cannot. Painting or the like might be.
London-Drill hall and armoury, $18,000.
What is the total cost of that ?

I have already stated to the House that I do not intend to spend more than $100,000 at London. Part of the site has been bought, but there are two more little spots I want to buy if I can get them pretty cheap. London is a very important military district and it is only fair that we should give them a good building.
Is it the intention of the minister to go on with the public buildings at Deserouto this year ?
Oh, yes, we are just calling for tenders.
I would call the attention of the minister to the Napanee public building. It requires some pointing, and some outside painting.

The chief architect tells me that he will be able to take the money necessary to comply with the wishes of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilson) out of the general vote.
Toronto Junction-Public building, $5,000.
Mr. SPI^OULE. Do you intend to keep that item there for ornament or are you to do the work ?

I intend to erect a building which will be a credit to myself and to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) who represents the county. I want to show that I have no revengeful spirit at all. I will erect a public building to his memory and to mine.
Will you erect it this year ?
lAs soon as the session is over I intend to go there myself.
Where can the blank forms 'be obtained for tendering on the public building at Deseronto ?

They can be obtained at Deseronto and here.
Woodstock-Post office, $12,000.
Have you a site for the Woodstock post office ?
Yes, the building will be completed in a few months.
Will this $12,000 complete it ?
Yes.
This will simply be a post office ?
It will 'be a post office, custom-house and excise.
It simply says ' post office ' in this item and in other places you say ' public building.'

There is a mistake in the wording of that item. We hare been trying to adopt the rule to call these public buildings, but I see the change has not been made here.
Sault Ste. Marie-Public building, $10,000.

iThis is a new building. I do not intend spending more than $10,000 or $12,000 or $15,000 at the outside. I intend standing by iwhat I have said a moment ago. I will give commodious buildings which are not too expensive, and I will" rely on members on both sides of the House to support me.
Ottawa-Public Buildings-Steel drawers and rollers, shelves, &e., $25,000.
The - MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. This is to replace the wooden shelves in nearly all the departments.
Where are all these steel shelves purchased ?

The Office Specialty Company at Toronto, and the Eclipse Company here, are the only places were they are made. We are offered American goods, perhaps cheaper, but so far I have made it a point to buy in Canada as much as I can.
Hear, hear.

Will they be bought by contract ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS-There are only two companies, and we have asked prices from both.

Is one of them the Char-leson Company ?

The MINISTER OE PUBLIC WORKS Oh, no, Charleson has nothing to do with that. St. Thomas-Drill hall and armoury, $7,000. Mr. INGRAM. Is there any* change in the design in the St. Thomas armoury ? The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. No ; we have made no change at all. Mr. INGRAM. I am going to occupy the attention of the House for a short time on /this item ; not that I object to the item, but when the item was up in the House before, I took occasion to make certain statements in reference to it. During my absence from the House the Minister for North Oxford without portfolio (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) read a letter supposed to be signed by the contractor Mr. J. M. Green, making certain statements which were supposed to contradict statements I made in this House. If that practice is to be continued in this House, then no hon. gentleman occupying a seat here will be free from such attacks as this. The hon. member for North Oxford said : A few days ago we had a similar statement made concerning another public work and made by a gentleman also living in the locality. But I have here a statement made by the contractor, Mr. Green, under his signature, giving such statements unqualified denial. I will refer to the statement I made, and see if the letter written by Mr. Green is borne out by the facts or not. He says that I said that ' a London man was given the sub-contract for the brickwork.' What I said was this : But I understand since that a gentleman from the city of nondon has obtained this brickwork and I suppose the reason is that he is a prominent Liberal. y Mr. Green cut the sentence off, and it turns out to be the firm of Page & Co., of Toronto, who have that contract. He also says that I am reported to have stated this : It was current report in St. Thomas that Mr. Green could not get the contract until he gave a pledge that the brickwork would be given to a prominent London Liberal. I made no such statement in this House : therefore, the statement contained in Mr Green's letter is false. The hon. xuember for North Oxford rises in his place and reads a letter denying a statement alleged to have been made by me here vrhen as a matter of fact I made no such statement at all. Then, again. I made the statement that if the person having the patronage of Elgin county would use the same judgment in this matter that he did in the matter of the Port Stanley harbour, no Conservative would be employed on these works in St Thomas. I say now that no Conservative has been employed on Port Stanley Harbour; and at the time I made that statement, I had a right to assume that no Conservative would be emploved on the	armoury works in St. Thomas. What I say now I can prove, that the gentleman having the patronage for Elgin county told this contractor that he was not to employ the Ponsfords to do any work on that building-why ? Because he said it would be humiliating to see those Conservatives performing any work on it. What did Mr. Greeii do ? He knows no more about preparing estimates for the brick and mason work on that building than I do ; and the great bulk of the work on it is brick and mason work. But finding that Dr. Wilson and an assistant of his who has a great deal to do with the exercise of patronage there, warned him that he was not to allow those parties to do any work on the building, Mr. Green went to Geo. Ponsford, a prominent contractor there, of Ponsford Bros., and to a man named Horton, and said to them, '1 want you to prepare the lowest figures you can for this work, and if I get the contract, I will give the lowest tenderer among you the sub-contract.' What did he do afterwards ? He got the figures, and peddled them all around this country. He went to Toronto, Ottawa, Hamilton and London, and tried to get other men to do the work for less than these figures given to him by those people in St. Thomas. When he found that those men could not get any work on the building, he actually went to the man who has the patronage of the county and said to him, ' Be firm, don't allow the Ponsfords to have anything to do with the building.' This shows the kind of a man this contractor is. I made the statement that the carpenter work on the building would cost in the neighbourhood of $5,000. My statement on that occasion was so erroneous that he has denied it; and yet what is the fact ? His own tender for the carpenter work is $5,200, so that I was practically correct in the statement 1 made. I want to say further that the man who has the patronage in St. Thomas has by his conduct deprived good responsible citizens of that city of the opportunity of securing employment on that work. In all the work that is to be done on that building, there are only two business men in St. Thomas who have anything at all to do with it ; and I have to charge the person who lias the patronage with being the deliberate cause of preventing citizens of his own county from getting employment on that building. And I would say that before the hon. member for North Oxford or any other hon. gentleman in this House takes for granted that a letter written by an irresponsible party states facts, or before he reads such stuff in this Houce, he had better peruse the records of this House to see whether such statements have been made or not. Had he laid on the Table the document which he read, perhaps there would not have been so much fault found with it; but having read it and put it into his pocket, he deprived me of the opportunity of seeing that letter or

who signed it. While it purports to have Deen written by Mr. Green, I think it was petticoat government that sent it, and not Mr. Green at all j and I think petticoat government dictated both to Mr. Green and to the hon. member for North Oxford.

I beg leave to have nothing to do with these local difficulties. I have given the contract to the lowest tenderer, it is being carried out, my hon. friend has been elected, he has defeated Dr. Wilson, and it seems to me he should be satisfied with his victory.
If I may be allowed to say so, if I were in his place, I would not say twice what he has said here to-night. I think ladies should not be assailed on the floor of parliament. We are all gentlemen here. I think the hon. gentleman has made a mistake, and I am sure that when he thinks it oyer, he will not do it again.

I have refrained on many occasions from using the language which I have used this evening ; but I have been pursued a good many years by these same parties, and I think it is about time that kind of thing was stopped. If there is a gentleman in that county who has the patronage, I think anything done with regard to that should be done through him ; but when other parties interfere who have no right to do so, I think it is time to cry a halt, and I for one do not propose to stand it any longer without repudiating it.
I am willing to fight fair against a man, but not against the whole family.
Well, when the hon. gentleman tries to fight against the fair sex, he will be defeated every time.

I will take my chances every time with my opponent with the fair sex.
Ottawa-Major's Hill Park-Improvements, &c., $1,500.
What improvements are you going to make there ?

The improvement of the entrance opposite Sussex street. There is a gate and fence there which are to be removed immediately. They are an eye-sore.
Clinton-Post office, $5,000.
Is that to be the entire cost ?
Yes, I do not expect to spend much more than that.	.

I am glad to hear that the hon. minister has adopted a policy which I have advocated some four or five years, namely, the construction in towns like Clinton, which has a population of 2,635, public buildings at moderate cost This is

the only plan by wbich tbe smaller towns can secure public buildings. Does the hon. gentleman intend to give effect to another suggestion that I have made, in order to save subsequent expenditure in the maintenance and care of public buildings, that is to have in the same building tbe residence of the postmaster, so that he may be the caretaker ? I think that the hon. member for West Huron approved of that suggestion.

We are carrying out that very policy. In several buildings we have arranged that the postmaster shall be the caretaker. In these small public buildings, we will be able to give lodgings to the postmaster and thus not have to pay a caretaker.
Is there a public building in Goderich, the county town of Huron ?
Yes, built years ago.

It is rather refreshing to see votes of this kind being brought down by the very men who, when in opposition, denounced in unstinted terms the policy of building in small towns of 7,000 or 8,000 population post offices and other public buildings. True, some of these hon. gentlemen have disappeared from public life, aud the places that knew them know them no more. But there are still in parliament men Who were most vigorous in their denunciations of this extravagance, but who are ready, as ministers, to submit similar estimates, and as supporters of the government, to swallow them without a wry face. In the town of Clinton the government are probably renting a building at a rental of $150 a year. They are now going to erect a public building in competition with private property, and which will depreciate private property to that extent. The hon. minister will not pledge himself that the postmaster will he caretaker of the building, and it will probably turn out that a caretaker will be employed at $300 per year. The cost of heating and lighting will be $200 or $300. The country will have to pay altogether, adding the interest on the expenditure, $700 or $800. And for what ? Simply as a bait to that constituency and nothing else. I do not blame the Minister of Public Works. He has thousands begging and praying for some government recognition, and in order to popularize himself and his government he is making these concessions. But this expenditure, just as in the case of the dock in my riding, will recoil against the hon. gentleman, because the public are not slow to form an opinion of public men who eat their own words.

I thank God that I have never made the imprudent speeches to wtiich the hon. gentleman has given utterance. I have always stood up for a fair and progressive policy,

and I believe that I am carrying out to-day the policy of my former days.
Kingston-Military Buildings-Stable accommodation for field battery, $5,000.

With the permission of the committee, I would revert to the Kingston vote, for the purpose of asking a question. I have heard that there was a great want in the college of proper accommodation for the cadets in winter. I am told that there is no skating rink and only a very inferior gymnasium. In fact, there is no place where they can amuse themselves unless they go into town.
We are now building a gymnasium.
Will it be simply a gymnasium, or
There will be no skating rink, I am afraid.

We have in Kingston such fine open-air skating that this, together with the ice-boating that the cadets have, makes a covered rink hardly necessary. The cadets can clear off a space for skating at any time, and open-air skating is very much better than that under cover.
Before this item is passed, is it any use to ask the Minister of Public Works if there are to be further supplementary estimates to provide for needed accommodation at the Toronto drill shed?
I am afraid that our estimates are sufficiently loaded for this year.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I do not see any item here for improvements about the two public buildings-post office and custom-house-in Gananoque. A drain was put down from the post office, and a granolithic pavement over it, but it has dipped so that it now has become dangerous.

The chief architect tells me that he has all the information on that subject, and the amount necessary for the improvements will be taken out of the general vote.
Public Works-Chargeable to Income-Public buildings, Manitoba - Winnipeg - Immigrant building, hospital (revote of $4,600, lapsed), $10,000.
Is this merely for repairs ?

No, that is for the new building, with a hospital.
Public Buildings Generally-Construction of armouries (revote), $28,000.
Where are these armouries to be built ?

Iam only a builder in this case ; I build 179
where the Department of Militia tells me to.
Is it known what amount these buildings will cost ?
We will erect them as cheap as we can- $3,000 or $4,000 each.
In order that the minister may not overlook it, I would ask him to consider the claim of the town of Orillia, which is the headquarters of two large companies, and which is a town of about 0,500.
Are these to be armouries for companies or battalions?
They will be erected at the headquarters of battalions.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Is the department going to keep .the arms at company headquarters also ?

In some cases it will be necessary to continue armouries at company headquarters, but, as far as possible where the regiment is compact and the companies near together, it is very desirable to have the armouries at regimental headquarters. I am bound to say that my view and that of the general staff has been modified with reference to this question. I may add that the cost of each of these armouries is expected to be about $2,000 or $2,500.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I am pleased to hear what the Minister of Militia has said. But it seems to me that there are cases, particularly in the province of Ontario, where some of the companies are scattered prettly largely, and where there ought to be a departure from the rule that the armouries should be at the headquarters alone. Our county is about seventy miles long, and the comp'any for the formation of which we are asking the minister for a sum of money, will be perhaps sixty miles from Whitby, the present headquarters of the battalion. The arms being deposited there, they will be of no service to the volunteers except for two or three days' drill during the season. This means that they will be practically of no use whatever. If these- arms are to be of service, they must be put in the hands of the volunteer, and the volunteers must be in a position to use them effectively. I think, so far as the county of Ontario is concerned, the amounts can be. divided up. Each armoury, I think, could have a certain sum given it for housing the arms properly, and a building for that purpose could be available without going to the expense of $20,000 or $30,000, for a building which would not be used more than once or twice during the whole season. I throw out this suggestion. We have seven companies in that county, and there is now a requisition in for an eighth, which will be perhaps fifty or sixty



miles from the headquarters of the battalion. These men will not he encouraged to go into this new company if they are not assured thajt these arms will be readily accessible to them for practice.
Where are these armouries to be built for this $28,000 ?
I have not made any selection yet. The Minister of Militia and Defence will tell me where he wants armouries built.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me what improvements he is going to make in the Brampton armoury ?
I understand there is a proposal to fit up a room in a public building for the armoury.
Have tenders been asked for that purpose ?
It is a small work, aud we shall not ask for tenders. I think it will cost about $1,000.
Will that be under the charge of the hon. gentleman's department ?
The request has been made to us.
I was informed that tenders had been invited and received in the department.
That is not correct, at least it is not to my knowledge.

I would ask the Minister of Militia and Defence to consider the claims of the town of Orillia for an armoury. In the county of Simcoe there is an armoury at Barrie which serves the purposes of the town companies, and if my memory serves me right, there is also one a few miles out In a neighbouring township. In the town of Orillia there are two companies, and right across the bay, in the county of Ontario, there is a company in the Rama reserve.
It has not been formed so far. A requisition is in, and I think in another year there will be a company in Mara.
There is also a company at the village of Coldwater, which is a few miles from Orillia. So, the armoury, if erected at Orillia, would serve the purposes of four different companies.

I would suggest that the Minister of Militia and Defence recommend to the Minister of Public Works the erection of small, neat, comfortable buildings for armouries. It would be as cheap, and far more satisfactory than the system of centralizing all the arms In one battalion.
Fittings, furniture, &c., for new offices for Surveyor General's branch, Department of the Interior, $15,500.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This $15,500, I understand, is to put in the fittings and furnishings for a new building being erected on Metcalfe street. I understand the government have entered into a lease for that property for ten years, at $3,000 a year.
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If I am any judge of real estate, the government, for the use of that building, is paying 15 per cent interest on the capital. I will undertake to duplicate that building for $12,000. I am informed the site will cost $5,000, and now you are asking for $15,500 to put fittings in this building, $20,000 in all. Why should this government pay 15 per cent for money when they can get it for 3 per cent ? Is that business ? I presume this is something like the Seybold building, and includes a rake-off for somebody, it cannot be otherwise. That building has been started since the House opened this session, the work is being rushed, and it is to be ready for occupation within a few days. The government could have put up that building just as quickly on their own ground, they have any quantity of land. I do not think that is the way to use the money of the people of this country. Because the minister has a friend that he wants to help, he gets him to erect a building and enters into a lease to pay him $3,000 a year for ten years. The minister said this government could not make a contract extending over one year, but here he has made a contract for ten years, and in five years he pays for the whole plant.

The hon. gentleman is altogether mistaken. In the first place, I do not believe that the hon. gentleman, who is a sound business man, I acknowledge, can erect a building like this for $12,000. I am informed that the contractors are receiving $17,000 for the bare building. Messrs. Ahearn & Soper are going to put in the doors themselves, and they are going to wire the building, &c. I believe that the building, when it is completed, will be worth, along with the site, about $25,000. I do not think I am exaggerating in making that statement. Those who live in Ottawa and know what property is worth will agree with me. I do not say that we are not paying too much, I have already admitted that the system that we have followed in the past is a bad one. But, I want to know whether I would be supported by the House if I were to ask for an additional million dollars for another building ? I do not know whether I would be supported, even from this side of the House, which has confidence in me, if I were to ask for one million dollars. I think there would be a pretty big kick.

Before we leave tliese items for public buildings, I would like to say a word. I was not in the House a moment ago when the votes for the Ontario public buildings went through. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) tells me that the vote for the Toronto Junction post office was passed.
I will be very glad to answer any questions that my hon. friend (Mr. Wallace) may put.

Has the site been selected ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS I intend visiting that part of the country myself and inquiring about a site. I want to erect that building as soon as possible. I do not intend spending a vast amount of money, because we have started upon a new policy, but I will give to my hon. friend and his electors a building that will be a credit to him and them.
I have not asked for a building myself.

The hon. gentleman will accept it, I am sure, at my hands as a souvenir of our cordial relations.
Harbours and Rivers-Nova Scotia-Amagadus Pond-Wharf, $2,000.

I notice in this list expenditures in Nova Scotia that there are upwards of fifteen wharfs to be built in that province. I would like the hon. minister to tell us what the policy of his department is in regard to the construction of these docks. Is it intended to go into these different towns and villages where private parties have erected docks, or where pri-construct public wharfs ? Is it the inten-selves by reason of the fact that no person thinks that as a commercial enterprise it would be profitable to erect a dock, and to construct public wharfs ? Is it the intention of the minister, starting as he is starting in this province, to go from one province to another, in towns and villages where there are private docks to construct docks to be brought into competition and thus render comparatively valueless those that private parties have constructed, or, on the other hand, if no docks are constructed at these points by reason of the fact that no person considers as a commercial venture that it would be profitable to embark in an enterprise of that kind, does the minister propose to go on with the construction of docks ?

I am very glad that the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has called the attention of the committee to a state of affairs that exists in the maritime provinces generally. Nova Scotia is largely inhabited by a fishing population. If the hon. gentleman visits that province he will agree with
179i
me that the policy we are pursuing is the proper one. These fishermen must have wharfs and harbours. Storms are very dangerous on the coasts of the maritime provinces, on the Atlantic ocean, and these fishermen cannot carry on their trade unless they have harbours and wharfs. We are not asking for large amounts of money, but I know how necessary these works are from my own personal knowledge. I paid a visit to the maritime provinces which has been very useful to me as minister. This policy is a policy that should have been adopted long ago. The fishermen require accommodation ; otherwise, their boats would be destroyed. A storm will come on while they are fishing on the banks, or on the open sea, and if they have no little harbour to which they can have access they will lose their boats and not only will they lose their boats but often they will lose their lives. I feel convinced that this policy is one which should be followed both by this government and by governments that will follow us.

1 may say in reply to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) who is objecting to this vote that these grants are not for towns and villages but for places along the coast where steamers may call to land and take in freight. There w-as a breakwater erected at Ingonish in my own county and during the November gale which was so destructive to the shipping in different parts of the maritime provinces the fishermen were as well protected as if they had been on the Ottawa river. That breakwater, I hope, is only one of several other breakwaters that will be built in the interests of the fishermen of Nova Scotia. I may say that the representatives from Nova Scotia in this House have not objected to a single grant that has been given to Ontario, British Columbia, or Quebec, and I think that these small items which are now doled out to the people of Nova Scotia should not be objected to.
There is no better investment of money than this.
Now, we have two statements. The one that is made by the hon. Minister of Public Works is that the primary consideration of these docks is for the purpose of accommodating the fishermen
To a large extent.

While the hon. member from Victoria, N.S. (Mr. Ross) gives as an additional reason that the steamboat people wish docks to call at. If that be the case and if there is some business to be done at these points, if the business is large enough to warrant these people in constructing docks themselves they will go into it as a commercial enterprise. If there is not business to justify them in constructing

the docks then, it is not the business of the country to erect docks for the use of these steamboat proprietors any more than, as I once before stated, it is the business of. the country to construct livery stables and hand them over to the people who may wish to engage in that business. The plea is put forward that we are spending public money in the province. If the plea is made for an expenditure of public money well and good.
I do not make my remarks especially as applicable to the province of Nova Scotia. The hon. minister is taking some votes in Ontario that I intend to condemn, and I shall do so when we reach those items. The hon. minister stated the other night that an application had been made in my own town for the purchase of some property there from a party interested in the property. I quite accept the statement of the minister, because I know it is a fact that these people are endeavouring to foist their private property on the Dominion.
Mr. McCarthy. Who are the parties who are doing that ?

If the hon. gentleman knows them perhaps he may be able to state.
Mr. McCarthy. No, I would like to know who they are. I doubt that it is so.
The hon. gentleman has an idea of them perhaps.
When we come to that we will have the facts.

This business of asking the public to intervene and construct these docks is reprehensible. It was tried on in my own riding and it failed. It produced an expenditure of public money, and if the government get as much benefit out of the expenditure of public money for this purpose in other places as they got in East Simcoe, they are welcome to it.

There Is no money better invested than the money I am asking from parliament to-day. This money is to be applied to help our hardy fishermen in the pursuit of their trade. Let the hon. gentleman give himself the pleasure and privilege of making a visit to the maritime provinces and he will find out that these fishermen are worthy of every assistance. We are not asking a very large amount of money and the benefit to these fishermen will be felt in every little place in the province. When my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) thinks it over he will agree with me that this amount should be voted ungrudgingly.

I am glad to hear the minister make this statement with regard to snaking the harbour sufficiently safe for fishermen so that they can approach them without danger. I understand that the policy of the government is that when fisher-

men require assistance for the improvement of their harbours, the Public W orks Department is willing to afford it. In my own county we have a number of fishermen and in one harbour they could not get in or out without great danger, and so they themselves had to make the harbour suitable for their own use. My own party was in power at the time, and I went to the Public Works Department and they said : We cannot do that, because it is a matter entirely in the interests of the fishermen. I went to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries at the time and asked him, in view of the fact that he collected licenses from the fishermen, would he not arrange the harbour so that they could carry on their calling, but the Minister of Marine repudiated all responsibility. I am glad to hear the Minister of Public Works fHon. Mr. Tarte) sitate now that he will accommodate the fishermen of the Dominion, and, when the fishermen of my county make application for necessary improvements in their harbour, I hope it will be granted.
When the hon. member (Mr. Ingram) comes to me with a fair application he will find me ready to give him a suitable answer.
It is quite right.
Will the minister apply the same rule to the Ontario lakes as to the Atlantic coast ?

There is a difference between the two, but for that immense extent of coast in Nova 'Scotia, we are only asking $179,000 altogether, while for one breakwater on the lakes we would spend that much money.

That is not what I refer to. The minister is committing himself to a principle now. The decision of the Privy Council holds that the inland fisheries belong to the provinces, and therefore the Dominion has not the same interest in them that it has in the Atlantic fisheries. The minister is building harbours for the fishermen on the Atlantic coast and he tells my friend (Mr. Ingram) that he will apply the same principle in Ontario. In view of the decision of file Privy Council, will he apply the same [principle on the inland waters as he does on the Atlantic coast ?
Most certainly. The fishermen are one of the most important assets of the Dominion, if I may make that statement. How many millions worth of fish did we export last year ?
About $17,000,000 worth.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Surely if there is a trade which requires protection and is worthy of our interest it is that trade.
I have no objection to it.
Why are there so many revotes here ? Why was not the money spent last year ?
We have to he careful and last year there Iwas a pretty large number of works for which no careful survey had been made. Moreover, parliament prorogued in July.
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the government should provide you with a pronouncing dictionary for these hard Nova Scotia names.
He is doing wonderfully well.
For an Ontario man I have seldom seen better.
With regard to New Harbour, this is the place we have heard so much about a couple of sessions ago.
We found it out all right since then.
Before concurrence, the minister should place a map upon the Table of the House showing where all these places are.
iOh, I have that map here in my desk. I will get it. There it iis, and every place for which a vote is asked is marked on it.
You .learned a lesson from the other day.

I know what I am doing.
Harbours and Rivers-Prince Edward Island, $43,450.
What is this Summer-side breakwater to cost ?

The amount of the contract is $55,000. It will cost a little more.
Harbours and Rivers-New Brunswick, $180,950.
Explain the breakwater at Dorchester.
It is under contract. The lowest tender was accepted, the figure being $27,700. The contract was awarded on the 23rd of last March.
What is the intention of the department respecting the Campbellton wharf ? Do you intend to buy the Shires' wharf ?
I believe we should buy that wharf of Mr. Shires.

I understand that the
difficulty is that it is necessary to pay
wharfage dues at both wharfs, and it is desirable that they should be under one management.
That is right. My intention is to try and buy it, but I do not want to pay too much.

You are taking a vote of $1,000 for repairs to Dalhousie wharf. My information is that it is simply wasting money to be dribbling it out in this way- that is instead of making these repairs, the department should make repairs of a permanent character. I do not know anything personally about it ; I am only giving the information I have respecting it. I am told that $2,500 or $3,000 would make permanent repairs.
The chief engineer says that this is to repair the present wharf; but I am glad the hon. gentleman has made his suggestion. We will look more carefully into the place now.

I would suggest that you instruct Mr. Shewan to report on the smallest amount which would put the wharf into a state of permanent repair.
Wharfs in tidal waters, St. John river and tributaries, $3,000.
Will the hon. gentleman give the details?
That sum will be applied to pay our share of the work constructed by the provincial government. Whether it is good policy or not, I am not prepared to say.
It is a most excellent policy. Has the hon. gentleman the details?
I have made it a rule not to pay for any work the plans for which are not submitted to me first. I must first see the provincial government plans.

I would like to ask the minister if there is any appropriation for a wharf at Gondola Point, in King's, N.B. ? This is a very necessary work, and I understand, an appropriation has been made by the local government, and I would like to know whether the minister has had any communication from the government of New Brunswick on the subject.

It is not on the list, but the vote is a lump sum to cover all amounts for the year.
St. John Harbour-Groynes at base of Fort Duflerin, $1,000.

One of the oldest, if mot the oldest, portions of Canada, the site of the old Huguenot French landing, is at the north of the River St. John, and is in a dilapidated condition. Inasmuch as it concerns the race to which the hon. gentle-

man belongs and the early history of the country, I would suggest that the government should expropriate that fort and preserve it as a public work.
The idea might be taken up, and I am thankful to the hon. gentleman for having suggested it. There is no question of race in the matter, but one of history.
Is there an appropriation for removing the sand bars at the entrance of St. John harbour ?

This is a very large question. I am asking this year money from parliament to build a suction dredge that will be ready for the opening of next season. With that dredge I expect to improve the port of St. John without an expenditure of too much money. It may be found necessary this year to do some work, but the larger work will have to wait until next year. I think we might go through the Quebec list, there is nothing in it of a controversial character.
Can the hon. minister give us any idea what proportion of these works in Quebec are new, and how many are already in existence ?
There is very little new. I do not think there are ten new works in this list for Quebec. Wherever desired, I will state as we go through them, whether they are new or old.
The expenditure on these wharfs in Quebec can hardly be for the benefit of fishermen.
So far as Gaspe, Bonaventure and Rimouski are concerned, they are largely for the benefit of fishermen. Besides, there are others than fishermen who need accommodation.
Are they for steamboat owners who wish to have docks to call at ?

Not steamboat owners. Very few steamers call at these places. There is a large trade carried on by small schooners in the Lower St. Lawrence.
Harbours and Rivers-Quebec-Hull-Landing pier (revote), $5,000.
Where is Hull landing ?
Just here on the Ottawa river.
Are there many fishermen there ?
No, but there is a fine population.

Throw it away.
lie aux G'rues, North Shore-Construction of wharf and purchase of land (revote), $7,500.
Why does the government place the wharf on the north side of that island ? The boats do not stop there.
Because the village is there.
Who goes there with the boats ?
A great many people. These people have no other means of communication. They are isolated. The least we can do for them is to build them a wharf.

I never knew a steamboat to go there. The island is very small, and the boats that go from Quebec to the Saguenay river never stop there. The only navigation they have there is with little yawls and a few sail-boats.
Are there many people on the island ?
Very few.
You might as well have some money spent there while it is going.
This work has been asked for for a long time.

I feel as the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) did when speaking of the province of Nova Scotia. We are building an immense number of wharfs all over the country, and I have no hesitation in saying, without picking out any particular place, that some of these wharfs are not as necessary as the hon. minister would lead us to believe. They will cost an immense sum of money, in the end, for we shall have to provide for their maintenance. But there is one thing in Quebec in which all are interested to a far greater extent than in these wharfs-the improvement of the St. Lawrence. I have no hesitation in saying that the province as a whole would benefit more by the expenditure of this quarter of a million dollars in lighting and improving the signal service from below Quebec up to Montreal, and in deepening the channel and providing proper terminal facilities at Montreal. I know that the hon. Minister of Public Works takes a great interest in the improvement of the St. Lawrence route. I can only attribute this very large expenditure on wharfs to the solicitation of members from these localities. But I have no doubt whatever that the province of Quebec would derive more money and more advantage if this money were devoted to the improvement of the St. Lawrence.

My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) must not lose sight of the fact that in this long list there are very few new works. Nearly all these works were built ten, fifteen or twenty years ago. My hon. friend will permit me to

differ with him. I hold that these works are useful. It is true that I take a deep interest in the improvement of the St. Lawrence, but take the population of Gaspe, Bonaventure, and the shores of the St. Lawrence. These people have to sell their products, to Montreal, Three Rivers and elsewhere. And how can they sell their products if there are no wharfs ? These wharfs are not only useful, but necessary, most of them.
Harbour of Three Rivers-Additional deep water wharfs, $25,000.
Will this finish the work ?

No, I think the whole work will cost about between $75,000 and $100,000. This is one of the harbours that are developing very rapidly. My hon. friend knows that there are large industries being located on the St. Maurice, at Shawinigan and Grand Mere. This work is under contract. I may say that the harbour commissioners have carried out so far all the work at their own expense, but they cannot do it any more.
Levis-Graving Dock-Travelling crane, &c.,
Are any of these docks or wharfs being purchased from private parties ?
Not one of them.
That is reserved for Ontario.
Ontario is a progressive province.
And it has a progressive lot of speculators.
What do you mean by a travelling crane ?

It is for working on the dock.
Lake Temiscaming-Dredging, $10,000.

There is a large amount of dredging to be done in the small rivers, and in the lake itself, and also at the mouth of the river. There are several wharfs built long ago, and in order to have access to them we have to do some dredging.
Murray Bay-Extension of wharf, $8,000.
Does the wharf at Murray Bay belong to the government ?
Yes, it was built by us.
Is any use made of that dock by a line of steamboats ?
Yes, Murray Bay has become quite a town, it is a summer resort.
What were the receipts last year from that government dock ?
My hon. friend, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, collects dues at these wharfs.

I desire to call attention to a formidable list that appears on P-183 of the Auditor General's Report. There is a list of government docks from which not a cent of revenue is derived, and I find among them Murray Bay. No revenue came to the Crown during the fiscal year 18991900 from Murray Bay, among a long list of others. It may be all very well for hon. gentlemen to go through the province and other parts of the Dominion, and from time to time announce that these millions are voted away without discussion. From this side of the House there can only come what has come to-night, an inquiry for explanation from the minister as to the expenditure, and a chorus of the hon. gentleman's friends ' Carried.' But, that will' not go with the public, and hon. gentlemen will find that throughout the province of Ontario, as they found in the riding of North Bruce a little while ago, when expenditures of millions are going on in this way, the public will ask for a little more than the shout 1 Carried.' The minister stated that there was a revenue from that dock, whereas the returns show that there is no revenue.
That is not under my department.

It may be a little consolation to the hon. gentlemen who are shouting ' Carried ' to an expenditure of hundreds of thousands of dollars, to know that the government is spending all this vast sum of money on docks that do not return a cent of revenue.
On nearly all these wharfs dues are collected by the Department of Marine and Fisheries ; I know that as a fact.
I would ask the minister if there is anything in the estimates for any public work on the Island of Anticosti ?
No. We have no public works there except the telegraph system for the use of the trade.
Do I understand the minister to say that the Island of Anticosti does not belong to us?
It belongs to us as part of our national domain.
As much as New Brunswick belongs to us ?

If my hon. friend buys a house, does the house belong to him or does it belong to this

country ? What I meant to say was that we had no possible interest to build wharfs there.
